speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow will be the first anniversary of the union of Newfoundland with Canada. I am drawing the attention of the house to it today because I shall not be here tomorrow. Through the courtesy of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), with other members I am making a formal visit to the historic town of Granby; a number of members, therefore, will not be here tomorrow.
I should like to take this opportunity to thank hon. members for the courteous manner in which they have received the members from Newfoundland since they came here as representatives from that province. I should also like to express the hope that the sympathetic consideration that has been shown Newfoundland and its problems will continue in the future. I trust that history will record the union as a happy one, and that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will continue to feel proud of the major role he played in making union possible.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin for the appointment of a joint committee of both houses of parliament on old age security.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, had the government placed on the order paper in 1946 this resolution to set up a committee to investigate old age pensions, I think they could have been commended for their action. But when it appears on the order paper now, four years later, the people may well ask what the government have been doing in the meantime. The people will undoubtedly look upon it as a delaying action. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) admitted that that charge would, in all probability, be made. I think it is well to remember that during the war the government promised the people time and again that at the end of hostilities an over-all social security program would be brought down. Surely by now the government must have the necessary information to enable them to do that.
Unfortunately the failure of the government to enact such legislation to cover our senior citizens is resulting in various industries being required by their employees to institute pension schemes. The cost of these schemes is included in the price of the goods that the industry provides, without the general consumer benefiting in any way from such a pension scheme. Whilst there may be,

and undoubtedly is, some difference of opinion as to how far a scheme of social security would have to go before it may be termed adequate, there cannot be any doubt about the need for the government bringing down this session an over-all scheme of old age pensions based upon certain recognized standards. I would say there is an overwhelming volume of public opinion behind the demand for such action. Much credit is due to the various organizations that have been mobilizing public opinion behind the demand for pensions for our senior citizens.
The minister took a great deal of time in drawing attention to what we are doing for our old age pensioners in Canada, and what is being done in other countries. It is a pity that the minister did not also, at that time, draw a comparison between the per capita wealth of Canada and the per capita wealth of those countries with which he made comparisons. I should like to have seen the minister make a comparison between what we are doing in Canada and what the productive capacity of Canada is actually capable of providing.
Let me explain what I mean by a scheme based on recognized standards. Most people believe a pension payment should buy the old age pensioner food, clothing and shelter. Most members of the house would agree that would require an amount of at least $50 per month. When the minister spoke in this house two years ago he admitted that $50 per month would not be too much for that purpose. I believe there would be general agreement, therefore, that the basic pension must not be less than $50 per month. Then, it must be all-embracing so as to cover everyone, without being subjected to the humiliating and iniquitous means test. This would enable pensioners to enjoy additional comfort as a result of the savings they may have made in the past, or which may flow from jobs they are able to do in their old age. The pension must be paid at the generally recognized age of retirement, which I think most members will agree is sixty-five. Then, as production expands in relation to demand and unemployment increases, the government could very well reduce the age to sixty, so as to enable people to retire at that age from the labour market, and make way for the younger generation.
On the question of financing, I realize that we are on more controversial ground; but if we keep on a broad factual basis, I think we shall avoid a good deal of confusion. The principle of taxation on the basis of ability to pay is widely accepted in Canada. The federal government have the income tax field, and they also have control of the national

financial policy. We in this group therefore believe that the federal government should assume the whole financial responsibility for the payment of the old age pension, and that funds for payment should be obtained in part from those with taxable incomes. I shall deal later on with where the balance might be obtained.
We in Canada have established exemptions from income tax on the ground that incomes below that level are too low to tax; that is to say, for married people we have established the exemption at $2,000 and for single people at $1,000. Apparently we take the stand that persons who are obtaining those incomes are obtaining only enough money to meet living costs, and that we therefore should not reduce those incomes further by income tax. For exactly the same reason that level of income should not be reduced by levies for old age pensions or other purposes. I therefore suggest that only income tax payers should pay into the fund. Then, at the age of sixty-five, all persons should be eligible to receive the old age pension; but to the extent that the pension exceeds the amount of the income tax exemption, the pension could be reduced.
It is interesting to note that that is the attitude taken by the Old Age Pensioners' Society of Alberta. I have in my hand a brief that I believe was sent to all hon. members. I want to quote from the first section of it, which reads as follows:
1. We want the pension age reduced from seventy to sixty-five years for men and sixty years for women, and the basic pension raised from $40 per month to $50 per month without the means test.
We want the standard of living that ia recognized in the Income Tax Act. That is to say, the ceiling on income in the Old Age Pension Act for a single man over seventy years of age is $600, but the single man over sixty-five years of age is exempt from income tax below income of $1,500. The married man with wife over seventy years old in the Old Age Pension Act has a ceiling on income of $1,080. The married man with wife is exempt from income tax if his income is less than $2,500. What we maintain is that the same standard of living should be recognized m both acts, and that the old age pensioners, single and married, should have their ceiling on income raised to the level of the exemptions on income for single and married as in the Income Tax Act. Both are based on a standard of living.
I think all hon. members will agree that that is a logical stand to take. When the committee investigates a scheme for old age pensions, I think they could well give consideration to this point. It would mean that no deduction would be made in the pensions of married persons with incomes below $2,500, and that no deduction would be made in the pensions of single persons with incomes of less than $1,500. After all, persons with
Old Age Security
incomes over that amount at the age of sixty-five would be able to live quite nicely without the payment of a pension. But in the first instance the pension should be paid to everyone, and then it could be recovered by income tax, from those with incomes above that level.
We are told that such a proposal would create a heavy financial burden. I contend that it would have just the opposite effect, that the payment of a pension of that kind would actually be an insurance, in part at least, against depression and would also provide security for our senior citizens. One of the main problems we face today is the question of markets. Lack of markets means increased unemployment, which means a reduction in purchasing power, which means a reduction in effective demand and consequently a reduction in production, resulting in depression. I therefore think it is of primary importance to maintain the purchasing power of the people at a level that is sufficiently high to buy the production of the country; because if that is not done, production will be reduced and unemployment will increase, and consequently the income tax base will be reduced. I therefore think it is of primary importance, Mr. Speaker, to maintain the purchasing power of the people at a level that will buy the production of the country.
When family allowances legislation was introduced into the house, it is interesting to note that it was recognized that the payment of family allowances would help to maintain the purchasing power of the people and would consequently help to maintain full employment. I quote from a revised draft, dated February 23, 1949, headed "Family Allowances-a Children's Charter for Canada", paragraph 4:
As the years go by, family allowances can help to reduce sickness, disease, crime, illiteracy, inefficiency, and other social ills that have their roots in child upbringing. Since they are given to people who will spend the money, they will create a continuous demand for necessities which will result in increased production and employment.
You will get exactly the same result when you pay out money for old age pensions. Money paid out for that purpose will be spent, and consequently will help to maintain a demand against goods. Hence, Mr. Speaker, when surpluses appear and unemployment expands, the government will be justified in issuing national money for the purpose of buying our surpluses. To that extent, therefore, old age pensions should be financed by debt-free money instead of by expanding taxation, which would have the effect of reducing purchasing power. In that way you would be stabilizing the economy of Canada and helping to prevent a depression.

Old Age Security
I was amused by a statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) and quoted with approval by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The hon. member for Vancouver East, speaking on old age pensions, reiterated the statement that was quoted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. But in view of the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare was specifically referring to a statement that was made last year, I am going to refer to that statement only. I would say . that this statement would undoubtedly be acclaimed by Wall street and by St. James street; and I cannot help thinking that every time a prominent socialist makes a statement of that kind there must be rumbles of deep belly-laughter in high places; because after all, if that policy is adopted, it means that you maintain a tight-money policy which bolsters the interest rate. Let me quote what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said, and it is to be found at page 644 of Hansard:
I must repeat however that, whatever we do, we must take care to ensure that any program we develop lies within the capacity of the Canadian people to maintain.
I am sure that all hon. members would agree heartily with that statement. He goes on to say:
In this connection, I will recall the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East as reported on page 469 of Hansard for October 3, 1949. It reads as follows:
"Up to this point I have not said anything about how a social security program should be financed. I am dealing with broad principles and not with details. I do not believe that I have any illusions about how measures of this kind are paid for. They are paid out of the national income. That in turn comes out of national production . . ."
He goes on:
"I say that, because there is an idea abroad that there is some mysterious source from which food, shelter and clothing can be paid for without taking it from those who produce it or have claims of ownership to it. There is no such way."
There is a remark that I should like to interject at this point. Unfortunately the number of claims coming forward at any given time are not sufficient to move your total product, with the result that surpluses occur; and if these surpluses are allowed to grow you will have either destruction of wealth or reduction of production, which of course means an increase in unemployment, reduction in production, a reduced standard of living and consequently a reduction in the income tax base. I go on to quote the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
I believe those words of the hon. member for Vancouver East, Mr. Speaker, deserve to be reechoed in this house. It cannot be too strongly emphasized that social security has to be paid for out of production.

Again let me interject: I am sure that all hon. members would agree with that statement, but shortly afterward the minister made an entirely different statement. I quote:
With that in mind, what we wish to do is to develop, within the limits only of the financial capacity of our people.
If the minister had said, "within the productive capacity of the people," I would have agreed with him one hundred per cent; but financial capacity and productive capacity are two very different things. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the hon. member for Vancouver East apparently regard the market value of the national product and the national income as being synonymous. They both ignore the fact that national income is invariably less than the market value of your national product. That is true of Canada. It is true of all highly industrial nations. Unfortunately in this country we have never set up a committee to investigate the question of the potential productive capacity of the country. But such a body was set up in the United States of America. A body of experts was asked by the Hoover administration to make a survey of the potential productive capacity of the United States. That body, under the chairmanship of Dr. Harold Loeb, made a careful analysis of the relationship between the national income and the national product. I quote from the report that was issued by the chairman in 1935, entitled "The Chart of Plenty," at page 71:
The total national monetary income in 1929 did not equal the total price asked for the goods which could have been produced by the plant then existing. But instead of dropping prices until monetary income was able to command full production, which is the classical answer to this situation, prices were maintained and production was restricted. Consequently national monetary income did net in 1929, nor does it today, command the full production of our industrial plant. Which is another way of saying that the national income was not what it should have been. In fact since 1929 the national monetary income has been commanding an ever-decreasing volume of consumer goods, and the actual national income has become but a fraction of the possible national income.
I would not bother to take the time to quote this extract if it were merely an opinion, but it is a statement based upon facts, upon a survey made by this body of sixty engineers and experts appointed by the Hoover administration to investigate the relationship between the national income and the national production, which showed very clearly that the national income is not capable of buying the national product. But that is only part of the story. Even if the national income were equivalent to the market value of the national product, there would normally still be a lack of effective demand, owing to certain practices which are inherent in our system, such

as the practice of saving, the re-investment of savings, and especially the plowing back of undistributed profits into new production, thus causing certain moneys earned by industry to reappear as costs before being made available as consumer purchasing power, thereby of course causing a deficiency of purchasing power to that extent.
That has been the history ever since the industrial revolution. People say: Well, if that is true, why did not the system collapse many years ago? Well, you have only to take what has happened to see how that has been overcome. For two hundred years prior to 1914 England maintained a very favourable balance of trade. Reginald McKenna, former chancellor of the exchequer, said that England's prosperity was dependent upon England's disposing of a certain part of her production in that way. The money paid out in that production, which was exported abroad and for which no goods were brought back in return, was made available to buy the goods that were left in the country. The same thing is true of the United States of America. From 1914 to 1949 the United States of America had a favourable trade balance of over $100 billion worth of goods. To a lesser extent it is true of Canada. From 1935 to 1939 the Liberals were in power in this country, and on an average we maintained a favourable balance of trade of $219 million a year. Will any hon. member say that the reason we did not bring imports into the country in exchange for those exports was that the people did not need them, when at the same time we had over a million people on relief? The importers in this country knew very well that if we brought imports into the country in exchange for that favourable balance of trade the people would not have the money to buy them, and the imports were not brought into the country.
I would say that the best example of the nation's inability to purchase the national product out of the national income may be found in the financing of the last war. Hon. members will recall that during the last war we maintained our production at a very high level, and the federal government found it necessary to take approximately fifty per cent of that production for war purposes. In order to pay for that fifty per cent of the national production they raised taxation to a very high degree. They borrowed enormous sums from the people-not merely the savings out of current national income but also savings of past income. And yet in spite of the fact that they taxed at a level higher than this country ever dreamed of; in spite of the fact that they borrowed enormous sums from the people, they were not able to obtain enough money from the national income to buy the
Old Age Security
national product. Therefore during the war the government had the banking system create for their use over $4 billion worth of new money, $3 billion by the chartered banks and $1 billion by the Bank of Canada. It must be quite clear that it is not possible to finance the purchase of the national product by money from the national income. On the other hand it is true that the physical costs of servicing the country must be met out of the national product. As I have already pointed out, the national product and the national income are two different things.
It will be remembered that during the war time and again it was reiterated in this house by the prime minister, the minister of finance and others, that no financial restrictions would be allowed to impede the war effort. The only thing we had to consider was whether we had the men and the materials with which to prosecute the war. Provided that we had the men and the materials available, we did not hesitate to carry on the production of planes, ships and other things needed in the war. But what happened after the war? As soon as the war was over we found the government going back to the pre-war mentality. Instead of considering whether we could do this or that in terms of wealth, we consider whether we can do it in terms of finance. The Minister of National Health and Welfare adopted that attitude when he spoke in this house. He said: "With that in mind, what we wish to do is to develop, within the limits only of the financial capacity." You never heard that expression once during the war. Nobody ever raised the question whether we could afford the money to build a ship or a plane. It was one thing and one thing only-whether or not we had the men and materials available to do it. Now we are being told that it is a question of finance. We have the goods all right, but we cannot finance the purchase of those goods. So, as I say, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has already gone back to that reactionary pre-war mentality.
I should like now to quote from a memorandum presented to the dominion government by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on March 9, 1950. This is a memorandum which, I suggest, should be studied carefully by every member. I refer particularly to page 4, where it states:
Throughout its history the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada has advocated that finance be the servant and not the master of the people. We strongly urge your government to take steps to revamp our financial operations. We note the continued existence of hungry people in many parts of the world and their needs for food and essentials of life. In Canada our producers are losing their markets rather than expanding them, only

Old Age Security
because our financial bottlenecks prevent the necessary adjustments whereby the growing chasm between our producers and the vast potential markets for their goods could be bridged. When we see such a situation we urge your government to find an effective solution to this problem of financing our home and overseas business. We are not prepared to remain as quiet bystanders watching the failure of our financial operations which, if allowed to continue, in effect will definitely assist in the spread of communism.
I do not think truer words than these were ever spoken. I am satisfied that if in future we allow surpluses to pile up on the one hand, and people to starve on the other, and permit a condition to continue under which the people who produce those goods cannot dispose of them because people requiring them have not the money we shall be permitting a very serious situation to exist in our country.
Some say that pensions should be on a contributory basis, meaning by that a basis similar to contributions to a pension fund on an individual basis. We in this group are definitely opposed to such a proposal, and for a number of reasons.
First of all, it would not be all-embracing. Those unable to contribute would not qualify; hence people in the low income group would derive no benefits from a scheme of that kind. I have in mind particularly subsistence farmers and small fishermen. Second, if contributions are on a compulsory individual basis, we will run into constitutional difficulties, and will also require complicated machinery for collecting the contributions. In either event the scheme would be greatly delayed. If on the other hand it was suggested that these benefits be available through voluntary contributions, I would point out that we already have that machinery available in the form of government annuities. My chief objection however to a compulsory contributory scheme is that people in low income groups require their total income to pay their living costs.
One point upon which I should like to touch before closing is that consideration should be given by the committee to including within the framework of the Old Age Pensions Act people who are permanently incapacitated, either physically or mentally. Some years ago the blind were included, and we believe the time has now come to include incurables within the act.
I would urge that in reviewing old age pension proposals the committee keep one main question in mind, namely the productive capacity of Canada, the ability to provide the goods required to meet the needs of an over-all old age pension scheme. If that capacity exists, then no artificial financial limitation should be allowed to defeat it. It

is time that once again the House of Commons should remember the statement made in the house time and again during the war, that anything physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible.

It had not been my intention to make any extended reference to the position thus far disclosed by members of the Social Credit party, and I would not do so now were it not for one or two observations by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) who has just spoken. I believe that toward the latter part of his speech he showed a very good reason for the setting up of a committee of this kind.
I find the hon. member using a number of terms which have been used by others but from all I can understand they do not use those terms in the sense in which he uses them. It seems to me one of the necessary things in connection with old age pension, or any other social security problem, is that we clearly understand the terms, and that we all have the same understanding of them.
I caught the hon. member speaking about "contributions" as though he thought contributions were pretty much like premiums on an insurance policy-or, if he did not think so himself, that he was under the impression many others did. Well, I, and a great many with whom I have spoken, do not hold any such views. It seems to me this confusion in terms is one reason for a complete examination of the question at this time.
There is of course a sharp difference of opinion among most members of the house- and I fancy most people in the country-and the Social Credit party, with respect to the manner in which a comprehensive old age pension plan should be financed. I listened to the hon. member saying, in effect, that family allowances, to the tune of about $300 million, have done much toward upholding the economy of the country; that when family allowances were instituted, arguments in favour of them were made in this house, saying just that sort of thing.
In his statement the hon. member is correct, because such statements were made, and I think they were sound. Experience has justified the making of them. It does not follow, however, that something which is true under one set of circumstances will be equally and universally true under other circumstances. "Circumstances alter cases" is an old saying in which there is a great measure of truth. It does not follow that because expenditures of $300 million through family allowance payments do good in the way described, that the same sort of thing, to the

extent of a billion or two billion dollars, would have the same result, only in larger measure.
Surely that kind of reasoning must have some terminus. If such reasoning is applicable to money, then I am sure it would be asked why it could not be applicable to anything else. I am sure all hon. members will agree that while a drink of whisky may be exhilarating, and two drinks of whisky may be exhilarating, and three drinks-I do not know just how much further I should go in the counting, but we all know that a certain amount is exhilarating-there does come a time with practically everyone when the amount of whisky consumed does not exhilarate any longer, but rather it de-exhilarates. It knocks out. I do not know just where the taking of whisky should stop. With some of us it should stop before it starts, but some can go on for quite a while. That is the kind of argument that is made with reference to these so-called "support-the-economy payments": that if $300 million will be beneficial in supporting the economy when paid out as family allowances, an additional $1 billion paid out to old age pensioners, with the money just manufactured for the purpose, would do even more. It may be that in the proposed committee an examination of that sort of doctrine can take place. It may be that by process of question and answer we can come to an understanding of how far our Social Credit friends would like to go in this direction. It might even be that the rest of us, and the country at large, could determine how much sense there is in this doctrine and how much moonshine. Personally I have endeavoured to be as sympathetic as possible toward what I have heard, but I am forced to say I observe more moonshine than sense in social credit.
In thinking of this subject of social security Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of a line of Lord Tennyson. It is an apt axiom to guide our thinking. It is:
Watch what main-currents draw the years.
It seems to me the "main-current" of the years at present is the movement towards social security. For my part I am happy to be living at a time when men and women are paying so much attention to this, and are seeking to achieve such a benefit for themselves and others. I suggest that the achievement of social security is of necessity a process of evolution. It has to come step by step. I think that is the case with all reforms. I suggest that the Russian revolution of 1917 was an incident that should fortify us in that view. The establishment of this committee is one of the necessary steps in an evolution. I certainly approve
Old Age Security
wholeheartedly of its being set up. I think such a committee can obtain and record all sorts of information that may be of great value to the people of Canada as well as to members of the House of Commons.
Since anything resulting from the work of the committee and other conferences must have the wholehearted support of the people of Canada, it is important that all possible information should be obtained. I emphasize the point for this reason. At the present time, when Canadian government revenues are not as luxuriant as they have been-j and they may continue to be not as luxuriant -a considerable number of people appear to be carrying on propaganda against what is commonly called social security, or, as they contemptuously express it at times, the welfare state. We see this not only in Canada but in a great many other countries. I believe the work of the committee can do a great deal by way of spreading facts on the record to negate this sort of propaganda so far as it is inaccurate or false.
I suggest that social security is a system to attempt to minimize the penalty for lack of financial success in our competitive society. Relatively few people can save enough in their most useful years to sustain them in the years when they are too old or too feeble to work.

I do not know why the hon. gentleman wants to make a speech at this precise moment, but I suggest that he should not attempt to do so right now, because I want to make one myself, and I have not quite enough time to conclude the remarks I had intended to make. As I was saying, relatively few can save enough to take care of themselves in their old' age or in periods of insecurity brought about by other causes. I suppose it is a fact that no person would be deliberately allowed to starve, but merely to have starvation prevented is not, as everybody will agree, social security. In my opinion social security is in the first place a recognition that those who have contributed to the national production should at least have the care of society when they cannot continue to contribute any longer. Second, it is a recognition that it should be received as a matter of right, and it should be received without humiliation.
In the motion before us we are only dealing with one aspect of social security, that of an adequate and sure old age pension. It must be that from the work of this committee a way will be seen to accomplish what we desire In the way of old

Old Age Security
age pension. The pension must be adequate, and it must be obtained as a matter of right. I think there is widespread agreement about the question of the means test. It must go. Contrary to some of the views that have been expressed in the house, I say at once that I believe the only certain way of doing this is to provide for old age pensions as a matter of contractual right.
Because I do not expect to be a member of this committee I should like to make some observations about the sort of thing that I hope the committee will discover and place before the Canadian people. As to the question of contractual right, it seems to me that when a contribution is paid, then we have the pension on that basis, the likelihood of any government having the temerity or effrontery to change the amount or conditions of payment adversely after the contract is made is reduced to practically zero. When there is no contract, the danger of reduction or changed conditions is always present. Some government will be more solicitous of its treasury than of the aged. The socialist government of Saskatchewan, having offered, with great fanfare, an old age pension increase, seized on the first plausible pretext to cut it. Socialists like to boast they are "in the van." They were in the van in trying to pare down old age pensions. Neither their act nor a somewhat similar act in the Tory province of Ontario would have been possible if we had had pensions on a contractual basis. So, from the point of view of benefit to recipients of old age pensions, a contributory system is by far the best system for us to adopt. There was a remark from the socialist benches a moment or two ago by way of defence against something I said, and it reminds me to point out a truth. We find socialists inveighing from time to time against what they are pleased to call the tardiness or the parsimony of the government of Canada. I think every person will agree, Mr. Speaker, that old age pensions legislation is not all it ought to be; but the record of the years can be searched in vain for an attempt by any Liberal government anywhere to seek to take something away from the old age pensioners, as the socialists of Saskatchewan did at the first opportunity.

His trouble at that time was that he did not know what his rights and duties were, and because of his ignorance on that point he was helpless, and not very useful. One might have hoped that the passage of time would cure him with respect to this lack of knowledge. Unfortunately there does not appear to have been any advance. Perhaps he is a bit like the Bourbons, of whom it was said that they neither learned anything nor forgot anything.
The hon. member also read on behalf of his party some brave sounding phrases from their platform. The platform stated his party was in favour of pensions without a means test. The statement he read goes on to say, however, that there must be provincial agreement about this. We all know, and the country knows very well, what the Conservatives mean when they talk about provincial agreement. It has been made quite plain in this house that provincial agreement means unanimity. They have made it quite plain that there cannot be any kind of development in the country unless each provincial government gives its acceptance of the proposal.
A short while ago an esteemed member made a reference to the entrance of Newfoundland into this confederation. Despite the fact he came from the opposition side of the house, he spoke in what I thought were felicitous and acceptable terms. Every person was glad to hear him speak in this manner- even happier perhaps because the words were spoken by one who was on the opposition side of the house. As a matter of fact, we who were here remember that the Conservative party would have carried this unanimity idea to the extent that they would only have allowed Newfoundland into confederation if Mr. Duplessis would not have vetoed it. The Canadian people have shown that they know quite well that, no matter what promises are contained in the first sentence of a Conservative manifesto, there will be a "joker" around the middle of it. Unfortunately for the Conservative party, the ability of the people to read is not exhausted after the first ten, fifteen or twenty-five lines of print in one of their documents.
I wish to revert to some remarks that were made by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about these contributory old age pensions. I believe the statements should be examined. This member has'indicated he is against a contributory old age pension plan, and that his party is against

it. He is in favour of a contributory plan only if everything is comprehended in it. According to him a contributory plan is all right for complete social security, but not for any part of it. This really means that he and his colleagues would favour the institution of several different sections of a social security program, one by one or all together. No one of these sections would be directly contributory. All possible sections of a social security program would have to be developed before any contribution could be required. It would be only after all sections of the social security plan had become effective that he, or they, would say the plan should be put on a contributory basis.
Just for example, take the idea of a pension of $50 per month payable at the age of sixty-five without a means test. This would involve a cost of $615 million annually, and in ten years the cost would probably be around a billion dollars. Family allowances are now about $300 million, and health costs account for quite a number of millions today. As soon as health insurance is introduced, we will expect some hundreds of millions more to be added to the social security expenditure. The socialist plan would be to have no direct contribution for any of those schemes at all until everything was complete, and then a contribution towards this social security measure could be exacted.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me this would be very difficult for any government to do. In the second place, the element of contractual right on the part of the recipient would not exist. I should point out, too, that even the socialists admit that benefits must be paid for by contributions or from some form of taxation.
If there is no direct contribution or tax, then there has to be payment by indirect taxation. If income taxes were doubled, it would not be enough to pay for it by way of ordinary taxation and they would have to revert to indirect taxation; that is to say, these taxes would be hidden and it would be denied that there was any contribution toward social security. My comment on that is that it is a most cruel form of taxation. It takes away a great deal from people who are least able to pay and it is just about the .harshest sort of taxation there can be. Since they know that pensions must be paid for, and since they say there will not be direct contributions surely they must admit that the way they would finance social security is by many hidden taxes. The people all the time would be gulled-or the attempt to gull them would be made-that they were paying nothing for this social security. I think it is

just possible that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can be credited with a smart form of political double talk.

Thank you. As a matter of fact I think no distinction should be drawn between these two terms. I think that one of them is an abstract term and the other concrete. They are not antipathetical. Social security is the manifestation of social justice, or one of its manifestations. In order to get a full measure of social justice you have to achieve social security. I suggest to my colleague that it is mistaken thinking that belief in one excludes belief in the other.
It is also objected-it has been objected by him-that people make sharp inquiries about such things as superannuation when applying for employment, as though it indicated a softness or a fear. I confess I see nothing wrong with this. I think it is a mark of intelligence, not a mark of fear. After all, what is wrong with people in this day and age

turning their thoughts seriously-and very seriously-and constantly, to endeavouring to accomplish a plan of security and comfort in old age? All of us can see the devastating effects of poverty. They are manifest everywhere in sickly bodies, stunted minds and problem souls. It is a fact that without help most people cannot possibly get freedom from that poverty in old age. That is to say, without help they cannot get what we call old age security. Here and there a person can struggle against grinding poverty, can make it sharpen his wits, can, through it, develop his determination and his ability. And so he will rise on obstructions to achievement. But where one triumphs over poverty a great many are broken or stunted by it. Hence it is no more than natural that people should seek constantly some means whereby penury in old age can be avoided. When we remember that one may succeed, we should not let the achievement of that one blind us to the breaking of the many.
We must never forget that poverty is wrong, vastly wrong, for it customarily produces those damaged bodies, minds and souls of which I have spoken. Therefore when people turn their minds and hearts to the avoidance of poverty they are acting naturally and sensibly. A person who thinks that way with respect to himself is using no more than common sense. When people think and strive in this fashion for the avoidance of poverty for other people their thoughts and their actions are simply applied Christianity. I cannot decry either common sense or Christianity.

speechtext:
There are one or two things I must say. The hon. member who has just

spoken did not think that Saskatchewan has done a very good job on old age pensions. Certainly we have not done as well as we should have liked, but I can say that we have done considerably better than his Liberal friends in Manitoba. In Saskatchewan today we are paying a supplementary pension of $2.50 a month, which is not paid in Manitoba, and we are also giving hospitalization and medical care, which is worth at least $5 a month. This in total is about $7.50 a month better than my friends in Manitoba.
The hon. member who has just spoken suggested that we had a means test on the supplementary $2.50. We have a means test, but it is the means test which has been formulated and legislated by the federal government. We are only carrying it out. I am sure my hon. friend could hardly object to that. The member for Winnipeg South Centre said to his knowledge the Liberals have never cut down the old age pension. Well, they may not have cut down the pension, but in April, 1949, when the pension was raised, I remember they cut the extra income allowed, from $20 to $10 for single persons and from $30 to $10 for a married couple; therefore I think the effect was the same.
As I say, I am not going to talk politically this afternoon, but in fairness I thought the hon. member should realize these facts. I thought it was significant that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. May-bank) spent five minutes dissociating himself from his colleague from Winnipeg South. Many of us did wonder whether it was significant that on the day before the Minister of National Health and Welfare brought in this resolution a parliamentary assistant-the member for Winnipeg South-was describing social security as a snare, a delusion and a fraud.
I was a little surprised too at my good friend, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith), the other day, when he said that there would always be a means test on the old age pension. He said that opposition to the means test is just window-dressing. If there are many Liberals in the house who go along with that kind of philosophy, Canada's old age pensioners may have to wait quite a while for much needed reforms, from a Liberal government.
The resolution before us today calls for the setting up of a committee to study this whole question. As many opposition members have said, the chief fear we have is that the minister and the government may use this committee, as a kind of stall or a political dodge, to avoid taking action. We have seen that happen so often in the past that we fear such
Old Age Security
action today. We saw it happen on the prices committee; we saw it happen on the flag committee; and we saw it happen on the Indian committee. Repeatedly in the past, the government has used committees of this kind as a stall. We hope it is not going to do so this time.
Several weeks ago the minister gave an undertaking that this committee is not going to be used as a political dodge. I sincerely hope that his undertaking will be lived up to, because I am one who believes that this committee could serve a useful purpose.
Like other Canadians, I wish today that the government was placing before us concrete and tangible legislation which would be of some help to those who need assistance at once. After all, a committee to "study" the problem is not going to be of immediate help. Nevertheless I can realize the very real difficulties which face the government in bringing about the pension reforms that we want. I think most hon. members agree that there are about three main weaknesses in our present legislation. The age limit, of course, is too high, the amount of pension is too low, and the means test is something which is pretty vicious. All political parties recognize those weaknesses. I believe most members of all political parties today wish to do something about it. The question which this committee must decide is the best method which can be used to bring about the reforms we desire.
According to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), several weeks ago
293,000	Canadians are today receiving pension assistance. I believe he stated that the federal government is paying $103 million annually toward the cost, and the provincial governments are paying $32 million. In most places in which I have been in Canada I have frequently heard three specific reforms asked for. Most Canadians want a pension of at least $50, an age limit of sixty-five, and the abolition of the means test. That is the platform of the C.C.F. party, and I subscribe to it. Under certain circumstances, I believe it is absolutely feasible.
What would these reforms cost? As near as I can ascertain-if the means test came off, the number of pensioners would immediately rise from 293,000 to 675,000. Again, if my figuring is correct, such action would increase the cost of pensions to about $330 million. Then, if in addition we brought in the other two reforms, namely the age limit of 65, and the pension of $50 per month, it would cost about $660 million.
Every citizen will realize what that would mean. It would place an almost staggering burden upon a budget which, as we saw the
13S0

Old Age Security
other night, is already bursting at the seams.
There is one other point to remember, and that is the fact that medical science has made tremendous progress since the turn of the century. If it continues to make the same progress in the next fifty years, Canadians may hope to live to the age of ninety years. A child who was born at the turn of the century, could expect to live only forty-eight years in Canada. Today, in Canada a male child has a life expectancy of sixty-six years and, a female child, seventy-one years.
All this can mean only one thing, so far as old age pensions are concerned, and that is that pensions are going to be even more costly in the future. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) stated that C.C.F. members are always crying for something for nothing. I say that is not correct. We C.C.F. members who want pension reforms have no illusions, as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has said, as to how they have to be paid for. They have to be paid for out of work, out of production, and out of the pockets of the taxpayers.
During the past week I received a letter from a trade union in the city in which I live. Last week I voted against a pension amendment offered by the Social Credit group, because it called for the deletion ^ of the word "contributory". This union, which is one of the largest in my city-I believe it has about twelve hundred members-has written to me, and I should like to place several paragraphs of the letter on Hansard. They say:
Our organization wish to express their disapproval of the stand taken by yourself in the recent debate in the House of Commons on the question of old age pensions ... We feel that the matter of old age pensions is a direct government responsibility, and cannot see the necessity for all workers to contribute to their old age pensions.
Trusting you will reconsider . . .
That union has done a wonderful job for the workers of Moose Jaw. Politically, I owe a great deal to it-indeed, I suppose I might not be here today if it had not supported me. Nevertheless, as their representative I must tell them that in my opinion they are labouring under a delusion and a misapprehension, if they believe that they can have pension reforms without contributing in one way or another to the cost. I wish they could have them without paying, but I am afraid the facts of life are otherwise. I have advised them accordingly.
I would like to see the means test removed right away, if we can find enough money to take such action. However, I admit frankly that if the means test is removed, it will probably have to be done on a completely

federal basis. I think of the government in my own province of Saskatchewan. I do not know what would happen if tomorrow morning the Minister of National Health and Welfare said, "We are going to eliminate the means test on the present basis." Such action would mean that the provincial government would have to pay a quarter of the cost. Frankly, I am afraid the government in Saskatchewan, and those in eight or nine other provinces, would have to renege, because they would lack the funds to pay that 25 per cent.
If the means test is to be eliminated-and I say again I would like to see it eliminated- it will have to be done on a federal basis. Otherwise the federal government will have to give the provincial governments other sources of revenue. It is as simple as that.
I said a moment ago that I believe the C.C.F. program for old age pensions is a feasible one, but I also say that I am one who believes it is feasible only if pensions are to be on a contributory basis of some kind.
I do not care what method is used, whether it is a flat levy on earnings, or whether the worker pays so much, the company so much, and the government so much. But I do believe that if we are going to have pension reform in Canada it has to be on a contributory basis of some kind. One such method has been advocated by the leader of my party. He has said that there should be a levy on all earnings above a minimum level, according to ability to pay. There may be difficulties in the way of bringing about a contributory old age pension scheme. The constitutional angle for instance has been mentioned.
I believe, however, that if there is a genuine desire on the part of the federal government, and a genuine desire on the part of provincial governments, we can soon have a contributory old age pension scheme in this country.
Let me repeat that I support the setting up of this committee, because I believe it could lay the groundwork for decent old age pensions in Canada. It seems to me that it is common sense to study the systems in New Zealand, Australia, Great Britain, the United States and elsewhere, to reject the worst features of those pension schemes, and to take the best features in order to weld together a system for Canada.
I take the word of the minister, that this committee will not be a smoke screen; I hope he meant what he said. When the vote comes I shall support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to clear up a statement made under date of September 27 last when the

Evening Telegram of Toronto carried a charge made by the Toronto labour council that "Rooney campaigned for 60 at 60 without the means test, and then voted against it when it was brought up in the house".
Under date of October 5, 1949, I received the following communication from the Toronto district labour council:
Be it resolved that the Toronto labour council condemns:
(a)	the attitude of Toronto and district Liberal members of parliament who recently refused to vote m favour of a motion in the Canadian House of Commons abolishing the means test for old age pension despite campaign promises to the contrary, and
(b)	the action of the Toronto Daily Star in suppressing the news of this vote in its columns.
And be it further resolved that we instruct the secretary to write to all Toronto district members of parliament who failed to vote against the means test requiring an explanation of their stand and communicate our feelings to the Toronto Star trustees.
Anticipating your reply, I remain
Yours truly,
Gwen Richardson,
Office Secretary.
My answer dated October 7, 1949, reads as follows:
Toronto District Labour Council,
167 Church street, Toronto.
Sirs: Your letter of October 5, 1949, received and contents noted.
I was sorry the Toronto labour council took the attitude it did in condemning people without knowledge of the facts. I also take exception to your Eamon Park, publicity director of the united steelworkers union, when he stated that I had campaigned for pensions without a means test. Never during my campaign was the means test mentioned.
If your body wishes my co-operation, as I had promised to you under a letter from me dated June 4, and addressed to W. D. Kearns, vicepresident, Toronto district labour council, Labour Temple, 167 Church street, Toronto, I would ask you to make sure of the facts before you put my name in the paper or pass any resolutions. I am enclosing circular dated May 30, 1949, from the Toronto district labour council, and I am also enclosing a copy of my letter as outlined above, in answer to same. You will notice that in my letter on your circular nothing was said of the means test.
In reference to paragraph (b) of your resolution I would say that the Toronto Daily Star was right in not publishing this news until they were sure of the facts, and may I be bold enough to say that it would be far better for your council to do the same thing. Over the period of years that I have been in the city of Toronto I believe I have done much to secure work for the unemployed, and it is my intention to carry on that work. I have never done this work from a political standpoint. I did it because during the trying times of the thirties I knew the hardship of the unemployed.
I am also enclosing my campaign pledges, and for your information in my campaign addresses I only appealed for the support of those who thought I had done a fair job for the people of St. Paul's.
Old Age Security
Anyone in the city of Toronto to whom I could be of assistance always knew that my door was open. I am your friend. I have always been, and I hope to continue so.
Sincerely yours,
J. H. Rooney.
I did not use the abolition of the means test as a campaign issue, Mr. Speaker. I never spoke on any political platform nor over the air on the abolishing of the means test. Furthermore, I never at any time even mentioned the means test in any of my campaign literature.

speechtext: Are you in favour of removing it?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
I did not campaign on the means test last June-and this is your answer-but I am and always have been one hundred per cent behind the abolition of the means test. I am not only behind it; I beg this house and this government to be the ones who will make it possible. I am, however, going a step further than my colleagues. I advocate $60 at sixty years. Members of the house are professional and business men. My friends over there are laughing at me. I ask you man to man whether you would hire a min of sixty years of age or over? You know and I know that you would not. I am besieged with letters and telephone calls every day from men who are unemployed. The vast majority of them are from fifty up to seventy years of age. They spend days, weeks, months at the unemployment offices. You and I know that the vast majority will never be placed.
Have you ever taken a look at a man of sixty years of age who has earned his daily bread as a labourer?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister should listen to this.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: Have you ever taken a good look at a man of sixty years of age who has carried coal on his back for thirty years? Have you ever taken a good look at men who have toiled in offices, shipping rooms, et cetera, from the time they were boys of seventeen and eighteen years, and have never got to first base? I have-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: Tell that to your minister.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
You and I know that the vast majority of men who have managed to keep themselves and their families in a respectable way, and still have managed to call the roofs over their heads their own by the time they are sixty or sixty-five years of age, are very lucky men. They are also very tired men. My plea for old age pensions is not just an impossible fancy. I base it on my experience

Old Age Security
during the depression. I do not think there is a man in this house who can speak with the experience that I had during the thirties. In the mornings, from 9 o'clock on, my room was filled with the finest of young Canadian citizens ready and willing to work, but what did we do? I am sorry to say we did nothing. Yes, we gave them a small hand-out every week, but if we had added another $7 per week and put them to work doing something, for example, building roads or power plants, things which we are now doing, it would have saved their morale, and in turn we would have had something to show for the extra money paid. We have nothing to show for the hand-out.
The city of Toronto has a wonderful island within its boundaries. We could have had a paradise and a great asset to the city. I tried and they said it was not practical, that Rooney was a dreamer. I acknowledge I am a dreamer. I dream that in some small way I can bring happiness to everyone in this great country of ours which has so much to offer but not people with enough imagination. You will want to, know where the $60 per month comes in. If we retired those who were sixty years of age we would thereby make work for those seventeen and eighteen and over who are out of work. If we do not, what do you expect these young people to do? That is the source of so much of the juvenile crime about which we hear so much today.
You will ask how it is to be paid. There are many ways. As an accountant holding the degrees of C.P.A., F.A.E. and R.I.A., I hope you will appreciate that I know bookkeeping entries. Let us think of Donald Gordon, chairman and president of the Canadian National Railways, who, when appearing before the royal commission on transportation, gave the following information and plans. He pointed out that interest-bearing securities held by the government amounted to $760,494,825.11, and that interest received by the government during 1948 was $21,627,032.82. Then the house is asked to vote to cover a deficit of $33,532,741.12. The suggestion made is to exchange the $760 million of interest-bearing securities held by the government for equity capital, and that the government should acknowledge an indebtedness to the Canadian National Railways in the amount of $300 million to bear interest at 3 per cent until discharged. This would be set up in the accounts of the Canadian National Railways as a capital fund to be drawn on from time to time to retire interestbearing obligations in the hands of the public, or for capital additions to the property.

I cite this as an example. Let us set up a fund, the capital assets for which would be our citizens and resources which are unlimited. I realize that during the last fifty years a steady and constant rise has taken place in the average length of life of the people and that life expectancy has increased by about one-third. For instance, a child born in 1900, according to the insurance companies, had a life expectancy of forty-eight years. Today a male child has a life expectancy of sixty-six years and a female seventy-one years. If medical science makes as much progress in the next fifty years we can look forward to a span of life of ninety years. I know that would mean changes in our economic life, and we would have an enormous new demand for certain types of goods and services. If we have to worry about what will happen in 1971, I say give Canada back to the Indians and let us start over again. Canada will be a great nation with a large population and well able to look after her citizens by 1971; and by 1988, if we have imagination, we should be as big and as prosperous as our neighbour the United States and have our own gold, which God put in the ground for us, to back our dollars and our obligations.
In connection with mining I want to quote from The Northern Miner:
This year the Canadian mining industry will reach a grand total of $2 billion paid in dividends.
Last year the mines distributed a record of $118 million.
That was more than the combined dividends of- all the banks all the oils all the liquors
and all the pulp and paper companies.
At present the basic pension is $40 a month at the age of seventy, with a means test. The federal government contributes $30 and the provinces $10, while some provinces are paying bonuses. According to my figures British Columbia now makes an added payment of $10 without the means test. Alberta pays an additional $7.50 without the means test. Saskatchewan pays $2.50 with the means test; and in addition all three provinces provide complete medical care and hospital service free of charge. I know the removal of the means test would bring in the remainder of the 625,000 citizens in Canada over seventy years of age, according to my figures, or the
675,000	according to my hon. friend.
This is a great country, but we must realize the fear of the aged. Freedom from fear was set down as one of the great freedoms for which mankind longed; but the fear from which the aged seek freedom is intense and practical. It is the haunting fear not only of lack of means but of facing failing health

alone without the assurance of some place of care and someone to care for them. That, Mr. Speaker, is our responsibility.
I have in my hand an account of the Moose River mine disaster in April, 1936, with which hon. members are familiar. All Canada stayed awake to hear news of Alfred Scad-ding, the late Dr. D. E. Robertson, and the other man who died in the mine. Remember, Mr. Speaker, there were three citizens; and all Canada stayed up to get the news about them. The other day in Ottawa a boy found some radium. All Canada was interested to learn what was going to happen to him. Remember, Mr. Speaker, in this case it was one boy. On March 1 of this year two miners and one mule got caught in a mine at Pottsville, Pennsylvania. Sixty diggers cleared away ions of coal, timber and so on, with their bare hands, and saved the men. Pete the mule was too big to get through the hole. At last reports they were feeding Pete and digging to rescue him a thousand feet inside a mountain. Remember, Mr. Speaker, in this case there were two men and one mule. I could go on and on, telling this house of the expense and work we would put forth to save someone in danger. Let us remember that we have
625,000	citizens in Canada, many of whom are equally in danger. Let us look after them.
I have read with interest the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) on March 10, 1950, in moving for the appointment of a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on old age security. I believe this is a good start, and I will await their findings with interest. I hope the proceedings will not be so drawn-out that this house will die of old age in the meantime, since 1 notice that the first committee of this kind was set up in 1908, while we had another in 1924. Now, twenty-six years later, we are to have still another. I ask this committee to consider a contributory old age pension of $60 a month at sixty years of age, without a means test.
I remember reading some time ago a poem which I should like to quote:
I hope some fellow will lend a hand
To help my mother, you understand, '
If ever she's poor and old and gray,
When her own dear boy is far away.
Let us help them while God gives us time. My hon. friend across the way seemed to enjoy himself while I was speaking. I have a book here which gives the history of what I and my associates did during the depression, showing the close co-operation we received in all parts of Canada. Also,
Old Age Security
for my hon. friend's information, I might say that the Save the Children fund in London, England, carried the name of Jim Rooney, together with the name of a man from India, for the work they did during the war. So while I am ashamed of my hon. friend over there who has been laughing, I should be very glad to show him our record in the city of Toronto.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, since time is short may I say at once that I support the motion. As all hon. members know, considerable progress has been made throughout the world, particularly during this post-war period, in the matter of old age security. Better standards are prevailing today than were dreamed of in the years before the war. Canada holds a particular place of world leadership in this panorama of progress toward better standards of old age security. We Liberals take second place to none in wanting to see those standards maintained, because welfare enterprise goes hand in hand with private enterprise as far as we are concerned. Today it is a competitive race, as it were, in the field of welfare enterprise, to the end that private enterprise may survive and that we may have a system of old age security in Canada, amongst other things, which will enable democracy to prevail.
I direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that there are on this continent two great democracies, one in British North America, and the other in the United States of America. This problem of old age security

Old Age Security
is one of strictly internal concern to Canada, but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is some necessity for setting our standards in accordance with those of the great democracy to the south, because it has always been the case that we must go shoulder to shoulder in many economic matters. I am adopting the comparative approach to this problem. I would remind hon. members that before Canada was a great industrial nation Canada was known primarily as an agricultural nation. In those days before 1920 a lost legion of Canadians were attracted towards the higher wage structure of the United States. That lost legion remained static in numbers throughout many years following 1920. It reached its greatest peak in the thirties, and I am glad to say the figures show that it has been steadily decreasing up to 1940, the year in which the last figures are available.
In 1940 there were 1,060,000 Canadians in the United States and when I say "Canadians" I mean people who were born in this country. Going back to 1930, the figure was 1,280,000; and in 1920, 1,125,000. It comes to this, then, that in the year 1940 we had something over 1 million Canadians in the United States. As against this, mention must be made that in 1941 there were 312,000 United States-born citizens in Canada. This reduced the lost legion, as it were, to approximately
748,000	Canadians. I say that this matter of a demand for wider social security today is bound to affect the wage structure of a young industrial country like Canada.
Let this committee consider what they have done in the United States about the question of old age security. Let this committee consider, too, what the United States may do within the near future. It is not my intention to tell the house at this time what the United States proposes to do; that will be a matter for investigation by the committee. But as the minister has said in his address to this house, there are some states in the United States that do provide old age pensions higher than the average in the United States, and higher than the average in Canada. The minister has referred to the fact that the average pension in three states of the United States is $60 per month. Those states are Washington, Colorado, and Massachusetts. There are six states of the United States in which there is a pension of $59 per month paid on the average. They are Alaska, Arizona, Connecticut, Nevada, New York and Oklahoma. This structure, of course, has to be taken in the light of the United States average which, I believe, is something in the neighbourhood of $46. I know all hon. members in all parts of the house were glad to know that the Canadian average monthly

pension for the aged stands up favourably in comparison with our neighbours in the United States.
This structure for old age security in the United States, Mr. Speaker, has produced certain direct results which are attractive to labour, business, and all others concerned with old age security problems. There is a federal old age security system in the United States -it is called "contributory" because there are contributions by the employer and the employee. These contributions towards a monthly pension yield about $26 per month on the average at the federal level without any means test. In other words, this is the basic pension upon which the whole United States structure is founded. It is the key to the pension system of the United States, which has enabled labour to negotiate pensions, over and above that basic pension, as high as $100 per month in the state of Michigan. This has been accomplished by the employees of the motor industry. Labour has been able to negotiate similar pensions in other industries throughout the country at roughly similar figures. It is this basic pension which we lack in our social security system in Canada today.
As for the remaining part of the United States structure for old age security, it is similar to the Canadian structure because we have on top of this a non-contributory federal-state structure similar to that which exists here between the dominion and the provinces. I urge upon the committee serious consideration of the present benefits at the federal level in the United States. I mention again that $26 per month which is available without a means test. I urge upon the committee the thought that this is a basis upon which to negotiate pensions in the various industries organized within the framework of the labour movement of the United States. I urge upon them the thought that there may be a pension of $100 per month negotiated by labour in Canada if we have such a basic pension in this country.
Before leaving my discussion of the United States pension structure, I should like to draw to the attention of the house the figures taken from the 1934 house of representatives report upon social security in the United States; that was about the time old age security was introduced in that country. In that report, there are figures which show the delayed benefits under the American system. These delayed benefits are benefits that arrive after 30 years of service, and 30 years of contributions under the federal part of the scheme. Where a person is receiving the average salary of $175 per month, after 30 years of contributing under that scheme, a monthly benefit arises of $51; where the

salary is $200 per month and there has been 30 years' service, under the United States system a monthly benefit arises of $61.25.
I conclude this part of my remarks by giving my submissions to this committee. In my view, the means test must go because it favours pauperism and snooping into the thrift of our Canadians. One more thought about the means test, Mr. Speaker. It must go because, in my view, it is childish. The premature retirement of our aged people from the labour pool is unthinkable in this day and age. One forces children to bed, Mr. Speaker, but adults retire.
The next submission I should like to make, Mr. Speaker, is to urge upon this committee to examine the world picture. In the British commonwealth, there seems to predominate a common age of sixty-five years for old age security. In the dominion-provincial conference of 1945, a lowering of the age to sixty-five was recommended, and I urge this age limit upon the committee. Finally, I urge it upon them because it is equivalent to that of the United States, which is the one country that goes along with Canada in preserving private enterprise and the democratic way of life on this continent. The last suggestion I make is to let the committee look into the United States system, with its basic pension of about $26 monthly, which will enable labour to do its part in its way to bring up the standard of negotiated pensions on the Canadian side to that on the United States side. Let them consider the states that exceed the Canadian average with $60 at 65. Let this committee find out how that was done. I am sure that no hon. member of this house, including myself, wants this committee to recommend anything which is beyond the means of Canada to pay. But nevertheless, in this competitive scheme of welfare enterprise as between the United States and Canada, we must consider everything which has been done in that country. The minister . in his address to this house was quick to point out that in the states of the United States where the payment goes as high as $60 at 65 on a monthly basis, these figures in excess of the Canadian average have been obtained by special contributions on the part of the states involved.
I am going to make a suggestion to one of the most co-operative men in the province of Ontario, namely, the premier. I think that when this committee report comes out, he will be able to gain much from it; and it is not beyond the realm of possibility that, in the light of this report, if this committee does its part in recommending the abolition of the means test and in recommending the lowering of the age, it will lead to co-operation between the provincial government and the
Old Age Security
federal government on the question of increasing our pensions by joint contribtuions between the provinces and the dominion.
This is the twentieth century, Mr. Speaker, and it has belonged, up to the first half, especially to Canada. Canada is an industrial nation and not the agricultural nation it was in the twenties. Let every hon. member be vigilant to watch the wage structure and the comparative social security measures available in other countries on this continent for those who may choose to go there. Let us keep Canada for Canadians. I think that we must go forward with social security measures at this time and maintain our place in the world panorama. I am not one who says we will kill incentive by doing these things. There was the visit to Toronto of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) and briefly, I say this about his speech: although he is a colleague of mine on the government side, he said "much too Mutch" for me. I repudiate his statements and place on the record my remarks here today.
Look at the United States of America! Look at this Dominion of Canada! A war effort was ours which knew no bounds and a war effort was that of the United States which knew no bounds. If you look at the maintenance charge figures of the United Nations you see there world production figures which reflect what the various countries of the world do in terms of world production. The maintenance charge figures assessed against the great nations of the world are as follows. The United States pays about 40 per cent of the cost of that great organization; the Soviet union pays about 6 per cent and our country pays about 3 per cent. Those are figures which indicate what took place on the North American continent; and the war effort of Canada and that of the United States was not killed or delayed by social security measures. Let us have no fear about welfare enterprise at this time in aid of private enterprise. Let this committee give us a national minimum of old age security within the capacity of this country to pay. Let them weigh the facts. Let them be the judges. We shall receive their recommendations with all due respect.

speechtext:
After all, Mr. Speaker, it is not the voice that counts in the House of Commons, it is the vote. It is not the opinion one voices as to what social security measure one wishes, but it is how one votes when one has an opportunity to convey one's wishes to the people of Canada. But it does look to one, even of a not suspicious turn of mind, as an endeavour on the part of the

government to postpone and procrastinate on this problem. Indeed it is not consonant with some of the promises that were made during the election campaign.
Many of the older citizens of this country believed that, if the present government were returned, old age pensions without a means test would be provided. Today there is disappointment among the hundreds of thousands of the older people across Canada, when they know that this matter is not to receive the attention of parliament at this time, but that there is to be a further postponement.
I cannot see this committee carrying out some of the promises made during the election campaign. The minister said that at no time was there ever any suggestion by any minister of the crown of the removal of the means test. That is as I understood his challenge. Well, I checked up the records, and I found that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) made a radio address from Montreal on June 16, 1949, over station CFCF, and that was pretty close to the election. This is what the minister said:
The government will do away with the means test for old age pensions.
That is contained in the radio speech as reported in the Montreal press. Then I refer to the promise made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) at Nelson, British Columbia, on May 29, 1949, as reported by the Canadian Press. He extended the promise considerably when he said this:
Provision of hospital services for the people of Canada and compulsory contributory superannuation are measures expected for the next session of parliament if the Liberal government is returned.
These two promises made by ministers were in keeping with promises made everywhere in this dominion.
