speechtext:
Today, sir, in this house one hon. member after another rises and [DOT] says: We believe in old age pensions without a means test, but we never said anything about it in the election campaign. Oh, Mr. Speaker, how this attractive promise was forgotten and not referred to is indeed an example of political campaigning that deserves the serious attention of this house. Those were the promises. Today what the people of Canada, including the old age pensioners, get in place of the carrying out of those promises is the setting up of a committee.	[DOT]
I rose for the purpose of suggesting an additional power for this committee, because the motion will pass. Since the motion will pass, it is the responsibility of all of us to

endeavour to give the committee powers to meet the situation as we see it in our country today. The resolution reads as follows:
That a joint committee of both houses of parliament be appointed to examine and study the operation and effects of existing legislation of the parliament of Canada and of the several provincial legislatures with respect to old age security.
I suggest that that does not mean very much. That information is now available, and no committee will secure any further information than the old age pension administration has today. Further on, the resolution reads:
. . .possible alternative measures of old age security for Canada, with or without a means test. . .
The door is left open there. "With or without a means test." That is a far cry from the promises made during the election campaign. I continue:
[DOT] *. -including plans based on contributory insurance principles; the probable cost thereof and possible methods of providing therefor; the constitutional and financial adjustments, if any, required for the effective operations of such plans and other related matters.
It is not with this that I am dealing. What I would like to suggest to the minister is this. In Canada today many companies are setting up pension schemes of their own. Last December the CIO made a declaration in favour of a retirement pension of $100 a month. In various industries the matter is being discussed. Plans are being formulated much along the line of the human engineering that is being done today through many large corporations in the United States. Yet in this resolution there is no provision to have representatives from labour and from industry come before the committee.

If the minister will allow me-there is no power to correlate their plans with the national plan. In many parts of the country today we find haphazard pension schemes being set up. When I say "haphazard" I mean haphazard with reference to a national scheme. Before this committee is set up there should be some declaration from the minister on behalf of the government of Canada as to the entire plan. What is the social security plan that the government has? It should not be done by dribs and drabs, by bringing in one measure after another, but by setting up in detail a national plan for a period of ten or fifteen years in advance. Once having declared that national plan, labour unions and representatives of industry should be brought before the committee so that their plans could be correlated and made
55946-90a

to fit into the over-all national plan. If something along that line is not done, and if the national plan is not announced in advance, by setting up the committee we are going to find ourselves in a few years with the national plan on the one side, and with company plans on the other, and it will be impossible to correlate them into the national plan. I feel sure that the minister would be doing a worth-while work on behalf of his plan for national security in the years to come if he announced it, because I have read everything he has said on the subject. I have read his speech, and I listened to it with attention. But I see nothing of a national plan. I see merely an endeavour to deal with these matters one at a time, instead of having a great panoramic plan which will set forth the objectives, the aims and the means. Having done that it would be possible to bring into agreement the national plan as well as company plans.
I do hope the minister will consent to the amendment to the motion setting up the committee. I have been on committees and I know that when anyone gets into committee and wishes to raise a question as to whether a certain power is within the ambit of the reference, he finds himself up against a difficulty.
For instance, I see no power to report, and I support the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in the position he expressed in that regard. The minister says the power is there. Well, certainly there is an inherent power; but there is no actual power granted to any committee set up to bring in recommendations. And if the government decides it does not want a recommendation that the means test be removed, then there will be no such recommendation.
That is the experience of every committee. In addition to that, if the government decides that it does not wish to have these company plans looked into, they will not be looked into. I suggest to the minister that he add a clause to provide for the convening, at the time the committee sits, of representatives of labour and of industry in those companies which today have company plans as well as those which have plans in contemplation, to the end that they will build their plans within a national plan.
I say that in all seriousness, because in the United States today the difficulty is becoming more apparent from year to year that within the national plan there is duplication with company plans, when such company plans are brought into operation.
In regard to the general question of old age pensions, our policy, the policy I support, is set forth in our party program. It is to

Old Age Security
this effect: A contributory social security program providing for retirement pensions at sixty-five, without a means test; and then there are various other matters not related to this motion.
No one need make any argument as to the removal of the means test. I think every hon. member would like to see it removed. Yet there would be no opportunity to vote on that question, unless the minister were to give his undertaking first that an opportunity will be given in that committee to vote as to whether the means test shall be removed and, secondly, that the committee will be given the opportunity to make recommendations.
If the minister will rise in his place at the conclusion of this debate and assure the house that the committee will be allowed to vote on the question of the removal of the means test, then I shall begin to see some reason for the setting up of the committee. If not, then it looks to me like postponement and procrastination.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us tonight a resolution calling for the setting up of a committee to study all phases of the question of old age pensions. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) introduced this resolution on March 10 he made an eloquent and stirring appeal on the necessity of having this committee set up. When we heard the echoes of the minister's speech reverberating in the words of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) we were led to believe that the setting up of this committee would mark an epoch in Canadian history. Some of us might be pardoned if, on listening to the minister, we thought this was the first time parliament had given any thought to the matter of old age pensions. One would hardly believe that old age pensions had been in effect in this country for over twenty years, but would have thought we were starting from scratch, with no knowledge at all of the subject.
The minister gave a long account, pointing out in great detail the various purposes this committee would serve. One of the first and probably one of the most important functions of this committee, we were told, will be to help the government arrive at a policy in regard to old age pensions. That is what we were told, notwithstanding the fact that this government has been administering old age pensions for twenty-two years, and notwithstanding the fact that back in 1945 they made it quite clear to the country that they had a policy which was so clear-cut that some five or six pages of the so-called green book, or the proposals of the government, were devoted to an outline of the details. Then for four years, from 1945 to 1949, cabinet ministers, Liberal speakers and Liberal newspapers all through the country persisted in telling us that we had not obtained the social security measures outlined in those proposals because of two men, Messrs. Drew and Duplessis. We were told that but for the obstinacy of those two men at the dominion-provincial conference, the policies outlined in 1945 would have been fulfilled. At that time there was no question whatever of the government being at all uncertain with respect to its policy.
Now it appears that the government just has no policy. Otherwise, why call for a joint committee to help them decide on a policy? There is no policy at the present time, in spite of the assurances given the country by government speakers during the election campaign of 1949. I have here a number of quotations from Liberal speeches made during that campaign, of which I shall read one or two. Here is a statement by Senator Roebuck. At the time he was not a member of the government-and certainly not a member of this

house; yet one would suppose that Senator Roebuck knew at least something about the Liberal party and its policy. The Toronto Daily Star for June 16 has this to say:
The means test by which people over seventy are denied old age pensions if they have other income was a hideous thing and he approved

That is, Senator Roebuck approved.
-a recent statement by Hon. Paul Martin that the government hopes to abolish it.
Some of the Toronto members including the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry) had something to say about old age pensions. Of course he was a new man in the Liberal party at that time, but we had every reason to believe that he knew what he was talking about when, according to the Toronto Daily Star of June 2, he said:
The Liberal party was prepared to agree with labour on its demand for a $60 monthly old age pension without a means test.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: How many years ago was that?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: That was on June 2, 1949.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: Surely not just before the election?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, a little while before the election. Then we have this quotation from the same newspaper under date of Oshawa, June 9:
The Liberal government plans to call a dominion-provincial conference to discuss establishment of a scheme for contributory old age pensions to start at sixty-five once the election is over and the political heat is done, Hon. Paul Martin said here last night.
That is a little variation, of course, from the policy set forth by some other Liberal speakers. There is not the slightest indication in that speech that the government would have to call a joint committee of the house, nearly a year after the election, to spend some time studying the question in order that they might be ready for the dominion-provincial conference. Not only were we promised old age pensions without a means test, not only did the government make it quite clear to the country during the period of four or five years that they knew where they were going and that they really had a policy, that they only needed to be re-elected in order to implement that policy, but we were assured that, along with the old age pension, there would be a national health insurance scheme. It is rather 'surprising to find the committee has not been asked to study that question. It was something which was generously promised to our people during the election campaign.
Old Age Security
The member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry), speaking in Toronto and as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of June 2, said:
The Liberal party will give Canada national health insurance. Our clearest policy has been on national health insurance. We are ready with it, and have a great legal mind at the helm to put it into effect.
The Prime Minister himself, speaking in Toronto, is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of June 15 to have asked his audience a number of rhetorical questions. He did not really expect the audience to answer them on the spot. He called upon his audience and said, Are you in favour of family allowances? Are you in favour of this and that? And then he finally said, "Are you in favour of national health insurance which we have instituted and have started to realize?" I do not know just what the Prime Minister and the Liberals understand by national health insurance. I am sure that the country does not understand national health insurance to be the paltry measure of assistance that is being given to hospitals and health services today. That was not the meaning which the Liberals gave to the term "national health insurance" during the 1945 or the 1949 campaign.
It now appears that, for some reason or other, the government needs some assistance in arriving at a policy with regard to old age pensions. The minister, in very solemn tones, informed, us that the country needed a committee. His statement to that effect will be found on page 636 of Hansard. Then, of course, he went on to state that we needed a committee to study the whole question of health insurance. I have received communications from well over 2,000 people in my constituency on this subject, but not one of them indicated that what they needed, or what they thought the country needed, was a committee. They implied in no uncertain terms that what they wanted was the removal of the means test now, in this session, by this government, and without any further delay. I am quite confident that the minister knows, and the government knows, what this country is asking for today. It is the removal of the means test now, during this session of parliament, and not to have the question delayed by a reference to any committee.
Apparently the government has undergone a change of attitude since it set forth its policy clearly in 1945. Just to remind the government, I shall quote again a few lines that have b^en quoted a number of times in this debate. They are to be found on page 37 of the proposals of the government of Canada to the dominion-provincial conference, under the heading, "National old age pensions at age 70". It reads:
As part of the general proposals now put before the conference, it is proposed that the federal gov-

Old Age Security
ernment will establish a system of national old age pensions entirely financed and administered by the federal government paid at the uniform rate of $30 per month regardless of means, to men and women age 70 and over in all parts of Canada . . .
That policy was quite clear. This country has understood that to be the Liberal government policy from that day until the time this resolution was introduced to have the entire question referred to a committee. There is some indication, in that resolution and in the minister's speech, that the government has changed its policy regarding old age pensions. Probably the note that is emphasized most in the resolution before us is the note of a contributory insurance principle, old age pensions based on contributory insurance principles. A number of the minister's remarks implied that the government is playing with the idea of establishing a contributory old age pension based on insurance principles. This would mean that each individual would pay a fixed sum, and would draw, as he does under an insurance policy, according to his payments. That appears to be the type of old age pension with which the government is toying at the present time, and which the minister particularly stressed during his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext: Nothing I said would warrant that statement.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
What are some of the purposes to be served by this committee? One of the things is that the committee is to attempt to discover the rate at which old people are increasing. We have to have a joint committee to find out that the number of old people is increasing, and to find out at what rate they are increasing. The committee is to ascertain how that will affect our old age pension scheme. Surely a department that has been administering old age pensions for over 20 years has full knowledge of the rate at which our older people are increasing, and has full knowledge of the effect which that will have on our old age pension policy. I fail to see what a committee of this house can add to the information which must of necessity be already in the possession of the minister's own department. We are to have a committee to study what those schemes will cost. The minister or at least the officers of his department now know what they will cost. They knew in 1945. There are three or four tables set forth in the proposals of 1945 which point out what the old age pension would cost Canada for the next twenty or twenty-five years under the various schemes of old age pensions, with and without the means test. The minister's department has that information. The minister himself gave us a table which would indicate that he has that knowledge. I fail to see

where a committee can add one iota to that information which is already in the possession of the minister's department.
We are to study the various schemes of insurance in effect in other countries. The minister went on at great length to point out what those different schemes are. If you turn to the government proposals of 1945, Mr. Speaker, you will find there in 1945 almost the same information that the minister gave us in his talk on the introduction of the resolution. There is no question in the world that the department already has all the information obtainable with regard to the various schemes of old age pensions in effect in other countries.
This committee is to find out just what kind of insurance the labour congresses want. Just a few days before the minister made his statement-as a matter of fact, it was the day before he made his speech -the Trades and Labour Congress appeared before the cabinet, as they have on numerous other occasions, and pointed out quite clearly what they wanted by way of improvement in the old age pensions legislation. There is absolutely no reason for calling together a joint committee of this house and the other place in order to find out what the trade unions or the congresses of labour want. This is what they asked for in their brief to the government. They recommend:
1.	That the means test be abolished.
2.	That all old age and blind pensions become the sole responsibility of the federal government.
That, by the way, is exactly what the government promised back in 1945.
3.	That the monthly pension payment be increased to $60-
That was what the hon. member for Rose-dale (Mr. Henry) promised his people; he assured them that the Liberals accepted labour's demand for a $60 a month pension. -as a preliminary and interim measure while the machinery is being developed for the implementation of a full social security scheme.
4.	That the pensionable age be reduced for men to 65 and for women to 60.
We submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is just no point in asking a committee of this house to spend time trying to find out what labour wants. The minister and his officials know, as does every Liberal member of this house, that the trade unions and all other organizations interested in this question from coast to coast have been petitioning members of parliament and the government for one thing principally, namely the abolition of the means test here and now.
Then let us give a little bit of thought to what is going to come out of this committee.

Again the minister will have to pardon some of us for being a trifle sceptical. The minister took great care to point out that a committee was called in 1924 and that in 1927 we got the old age pension as a result of that committee. That suggests something to me. I, of course, may be somewhat critical; but that fact suggests to me that we are to get a committee now in 1950, as in the 1920's, and three years from now or in 1953 we shall be ready to abolish the means test or we shall be ready with a new scheme for old age pensions. By the time we get a committee and that committee takes the time necessary to go into all those fields of study that the minister outlined, and then by the time we get a dominion-provincial conference and get their agreement to a contributory old age scheme, get the legislation ready and get the legislation through the house, it looks as though it will be 1953, a most appropriate time for the introduction of an improvement in the old age pensions legislation.

speechtext: Just before the next election!

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I stated once before in this house, the withholding of much needed social legislation until the eve of an election has over the years become the standard practice of this government. In 1945 it was family allowances. The legislation was passed and the cheques were all ready before the election was announced. All we had to do was to vote Liberal and the cheques would be mailed out. In 1949 it was not necessary to introduce any great scheme of social security. The government had plenty of money to mail out to the voters throughout the country without having to rely upon any improvement in social security. There were a few hundred million dollars in compulsory savings that were passed out in April, just before the election in June. That was a very appropriate time. It just happened, of course, that the time had rolled around for those cheques to be mailed. Then, of course, there were other hundreds of millions to be mailed out to the western farmers for their wheat crops of the three preceding years. That was a very appropriate time. It was all purely incidental, of course; it was all just a matter of course, a matter of no particular planning on the part of the government, to have those payments made just before the election. We would not accuse them of that. But the point is that here we have in Canada a crying need for an advance in social legislation to the point at least of removing the means test, and we have the government taking steps that will of necessity delay this social security until we come to the eve of another general election.
Old Age Security
On the whole question of the means test I want to take just a few minutes. The means test today is regarded by the trade union movement, by labour, by the old age pensioners and by the Canadian public generally, to use the words of the Old Age Pensioners' Society of Manitoba, as one of the most iniquitous pieces of legislation that could be enacted by any government against its citizens. It creates a feeling of inequality, a feeling of dissatisfaction, and a feeling 'of suffering on the part of a great many people; it creates the kind of feeling that breeds communism.
If you want to breed communism in this country, continue to leave a large section of our people feeling that they are being discriminated against, and a large section of the public agreeing with them. If you do that you will be doing the very thing that will bring communism. In a country where freedom of enterprise is the watchword of our government, a government that prides itself on its support of free enterprise, one wonders when one sees the older citizens reduced to what amounts to a form of slavery. These older people must not earn more than a few extra dollars above their pension which, even with that pension, constitutes but a pittance, and is far from a reasonable standard of living. They cannot accept full or even parttime employment over any prolonged period of time. They have no freedom. They are regimented by a government that accuses other parties of regimentation. There is no country in the world today where older people are regimented more than they are under the means test which is in effect in this country. They dare not live in a respectable apartment, even if some friend wants to pay the rent for them, or a relative wants to do so. They dare not have more than a few dollars in the bank. They are not free men and women. As far as this country is concerned, this is not for our older citizens a free country, even though we are governed by a party and a government that prides itself on its free enterprise.
These older people cannot accept gifts from relatives or friends. They are discouraged from saving. If they save or accumulate a little they are penalized when they reach the age at which they go on old age pension. The means test reduces our older citizens to a state of pauperism, and leaves them the objects of pity, which, I submit, Mr. Speaker, is a condition that should not prevail in this country. There just is no excuse for the government dallying with this question until we come to the time when we are on the eve of another general election. It is unfair; it is cruel to these older people to pass this subject off to a committee that will require months

Old Age Security
and months to complete the study that is outlined to them; to bring the matter before the dominion-provincial conference; to reach an agreement with the provinces, and to get legislation through this house. The whole thing cannot be done in less than two or possibly three sessions of parliament. In the meantime the country is clamouring for the removal of the means test here and now. That, Mr. Speaker, is what this country and the people waht, and not, as the minister says, a committee.
A few days ago I picked up this special notice in one of the Toronto papers. It is called "sacrificial luncheon." It is a luncheon provided by Carlton Street United Church in Toronto. This is the notice:
All women of the church are invited to a sacrificial luncheon, Wednesday. April 5, in the assembly hall. The free-will offering of this luncheon will go directly to the benevolent fund of Carlton Street United Church, which provides hot dinners for 2,500 old age pensioners in that district.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this country is not reduced to that state of privation where it is necessary, or should be necessary, for any organization to have to provide hot lunches for 2,500 old age pensioners in one city, whose pensions and whose incomes are not sufficient to enable them to provide themselves with hot lunches. That I say is a disgrace to this country and to this government.
Here is a quotation from the Veterans Advocate:
It is our opinion that the means test puts a penalty on thrift and a premium on improvidence. The applicant who has made no provision for old age is eligible for pension, without question and without difficulty. His thrifty and hard-working neighbour has to pass a diabolical means test before his application is considered.
The wastrel is too often in a better state than the industrious and ambitious who scrimp and save for old age, but who never achieve complete financial independence.
To iron out inequality, we would prefer to see old age pensions, without means test, applied universally at age 65. The family allowance act is a bonus to every new citizen at birth. It is based in a measure on a potential contribution made to the country's welfare. We take the young on faith and hope. The other and greater virtue should not be withheld from the old nor if extended should it be niggardly, mean and circumscribed.
It will be a long time before old age pensions can be placed on a contributory basis. Till such time this country cannot afford to be ungenerous to those older citizens, who have little but memory to live on.
I have time for one more short quotation from the News-Herald of Vancouver.
The time is coming when old age pensions will have to be given to everyone, as family allowances are today. Rich and poor alike will receive them and those with incomes over a certain minimum will pay them back in income tax. This will take a lot of bookkeeping, but it will remove the stigma that for some strange reason some people still

attach to old age pensions. Many an old person is bitterly ashamed taking the pension and does his best to keep it a dark secret. This shouldn't be necessary.
I submit that what we should be considering at this time is how we can abolish the means test, or failing that how we can raise the ceiling on the earnings and income which old age pensioners may receive. These are two reforms one of which at least could be effected now and should be effected now. One is the removal of the means test, the other, the raising of the ceiling, as was already stated this afternoon, to $1,500 for single people, and $2,500 for married people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing a constituency in which there is a very high percentage of elderly people, who live in that area on account of our usually mild winter climate, I should like to say a few words on behalf of those who are resident in my constituency and then I wish to say a few more words regarding a much larger group of elderly citizens who reside in every part of Canada. In the first place I must express some regret that the government has not seen fit to keep the election promises we have heard quoted, and to bring in some definite old age security legislation at the present time. However, seeing that the government is not prepared to do this, and that it intends to set up a committee, I am pleased to note that the committee is to be given wide scope.
At page 635 of Hansard, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), when introducing the resolution, stated that the committee would study the operation and effects of existing legislation of the parliament of Canada, and of the several provincial legislatures, with respect to old age security, similar legislation in other countries and possible alternative measures of old age security for Canada with or without a means test. Then the minister went on to say that this committee-*
-is to develop the best possible old age and retirement system that can be devised, with full consideration for the well-being of all Canadians. This proposed joint committee can do a real public service by its investigations in clearing the way for a better system of pensions, if that is thought desirable, after analysis, for our senior aged citizens.
Two years ago, at the annual convention of the Canadian Legion, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs described the War Veterans Allowance Act as being a form of old age security, or old age pension, which was made applicable to men who had aged prematurely by service in an actual theatre of war during the first and second world wars. Because it was a recognized fact that men who had seen service in the trenches had aged prematurely, an old age pension-it was then called a burnt-out

pension, in the early years of the legislation- would be made applicable to veterans five years earlier than when pensions would be granted to the aged people of the country who had not seen service overseas.
May I ask the minister whether it is his intention to investigate, as one of the systems of old age pensions, the War Veterans Allowance Act, and to see how that will fit into his scheme for the new old age pension. Will those matters be referred to this committee?. Hon. members on this side of the house have asked and pleaded for the setting up of a committee on veterans affairs. That request has been forwarded to all of us through innumerable branches of the Legion. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) has seen fit to say that no such committee will be set up.
Many of the problems which affect the aged civilian citizens affect the aged veteran. So far as the application of the War Veterans Allowance Act is concerned, the same problems appear continually. Representations have been made by the Canadian Legion for the removal of the means test. Representations have been made toy the same organization for an increase in the basic allowance, so that that basic allowance may be brought in line with the old age pension schemes of the several provinces.
Representatives of the organized bodies of veterans will not have an opportunity of appearing before a special committee on veterans affairs. In view of this fact, and the fact that this committee is now being set up with the idea of providing the best possible pension scheme for all Canadians, will there be an opportunity for veterans to appear before this committee in exactly the same way as the minister intimated this afternoon that industrialists will be able to appear, and in exactly the same way as he intimated that representatives of labour would be able to appear? I am asking whether veterans, or the representatives of veterans, will be able to appear before the committee and point out to the representative members of the House of Commons serving on that committee why it is so desirable that the means test be removed' from the old age pension the veterans are receiving, and why it is desirable that the basic allowance should be increased. Will they be permitted to make their representations in exactly the same way as will organized labour and industrialists who are to be permitted to come before the committee and point out why certain matters should be dealt with and considered by this wide and all-embracing committee of this House of Commons, which the minister is
Old Age Security
setting up in the hope of being able to devise the best possible old age pension scheme for all Canadians?
I admit that at the present time the federal government is paying all the war veterans allowances, and that the provinces have not been asked to make contributions in that respect. But that is only one of the many matters which could be discussed. Therefore I should like very much to hear what the minister has to say with respect to the opportunity to be given the veterans of this land to place their problems of old age before this special old age committee. I believe it is most important that they have this opportunity, in view of the fact that they have been denied the privilege of appearing before a special veterans committee of the House of Commons.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in connection with the setting up of this committee to consider old age pensions. As hon. members will know, a resolution stands on the order paper in my name this session, as it did at the last one. For certain reasons I did not present the resolution to the house at the last session. At this session the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has placed this motion before the house to send the matter to a special committee for consideration. I am satisfied to wait until this is done and, if it brings in recommendations satisfactory to the old people I represent, I shall be for it. If it does not, then I shall have to have a chance to speak again with respect to it.
The resolution on the order paper at this session is in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of introducing an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act so that it would be on a contributory basis with no means test and paid to all persons reaching the age of sixty-five years.
I believe I should have said that it should be compulsory, because it is my view that we will never have a proper old age pension scheme as it is now. Mr. Ilsley said some years ago that that is the only way it would ever work, and I am of the same opinion. I would hope, however, that those in charge of this matter will not dilly-dally too long, until I am dead, and all the other old people are dead. I hope the committee will bring in a proper recommendation, so that the old people will be treated properly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in the debate at this stage I feel like someone who attempts to gnaw meat from a bone from which most of the meat has been consumed. I wish to

Old Age Security
make a few observations on the resolution and certain aspects of the financing of old age pensions which will be considered by this committee. For a few minutes I want to discuss the right of Canadian citizens to old age security, and the abolition of the means test. First of all I believe the resolution should call for consideration by the committee of overall security instead of being confined to one aspect thereof, the question of old age pensions. In my opinion there is no question that the country is waiting for the government to give consideration to a scheme of over-all security covering all Canadians. That is evidenced by resolutions passed by labour organizations across Canada, by both labour congresses and local labour organizations, by veterans' organizations, by farmers' organizations and by innumerable women's organizations. In addition to that, we find at the present time proposals for over-all social security in the platform of every political party in this house. Therefore there is no question that the country is waiting for the government to give consideration to the question of over-all security.
During recent weeks I think most hon. members of the house have realized more fully than ever that opposition to the means test is growing rapidly. I might say that even the Liberal government expressed the opinion in 1945 that the means test was undesirable. At page 37 of the proposals of the dominion government I find this under the heading, "deficiencies of the present scheme":
The means test is generally recognized as undesirable after a certain age. It has been noted that about forty per cent of all persons of seventy years of age and over make application, satisfy the means test requirements and receive the pension. There is little doubt that a very considerable number in addition are not able entirely to support themselves, but are dependent upon their families, and refrain from applying for pensions because of the embarrassment occasioned by the means test.
I think it is generally recognized by the majority of Canadians-

speechtext:
-that the means test as it is imposed at the present time is a penalty on thrift, is unfair and is most unfortunate for those people who have small savings, industrial pensions, annuities and so on. During the last two or three weeks I have received dozens of letters from persons with small incomes, life savings, annuities or industrial pensions who cannot take advantage of the old age pension scheme and yet have not enough to live on.
I want to refer for a minute or two to the percentage of our population making provision for old age. In doing so I should like

to refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on March 3, 1949. I suggest that anyone who is interested in the statistical aspects of the question should read the speech made by the hon. member on that date. I understand the figures used therein were largely supplied by the research division of the minister's department. What do we find? At that date there were in Canada a total of 829,936 who were making provision for old age. We also find according to these figures that the population between the ages of 20 and 60 years totalled 6,676,700. That means that about 13 per cent of the people of Canada are making some provision for their old age. You may question these figures because of the increase in population and so on, but I am quite sure that the minister will agree it is safe to say that not more than 15 per cent of the people of Canada are able to make provision for their old age.
That is the problem facing the house and the committee, and it is a serious and important one. These are several approaches to the question of old age security. In the main we find there are two plans put forward by members of the house and by people outside the house. The first is some scheme of compulsory contributions based on the insurance principle. The second is the payment of old age pensions from taxation based on ability to pay. I think those who know me and my attitude to many questions in this house will realize that I am not given to advancing unsound financial proposals unsound schemes, or giving voice to Utopian ideas. I am pleased to note that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) is listening with interest, and I trust on this occasion with considerable agreement.

speechtext:
I favour payment from taxation mainly for two reasons. First, I believe it is unfair and unjust to collect contributions on an equal basis from the people of the country under the insurance principle to build up old age security. This afternoon, and in previous debates on this question, a good many members have said that they believe in the abolition of the means test. That does not mean a thing if you say at the same time that you believe in a compulsory contributory scheme based on the insurance principle. All you are saying is that you are going to give the people of Canada an opportunity to buy a life annuity or insure themselves against old age, and the government will be willing to accept the cost of administration. The bare fact of the matter is that would mean many

people would be worse off than they are at the present time. It would simply mean that the government would spend $4 million or $5 million for administration and save $100 million at this time.
Throughout the ages it has been the accepted duty of the working population to care for the aged. Under the conditions that prevailed years ago, and possibly even up to recent years, it was much easier to do that than it is today. For instance, on the farms years ago there was ample room. Old people assisted with odd jobs. Costs of living were lower; standards of living were lower; and in the towns there was. more room than there is today. People were not living in flats, small suites and crowded quarters. Odd jobs were available for older people under conditions which are not present today. Life generally was much less complicated and wants simple.
I want to emphasize that by paying taxes today for old age pensions we are only doing jointly and collectively what has been done individually for ages, namely, caring for the aged out of current production. I consider that is our duty, and this duty has scriptural authority for those who view life from that point of view. In my opinion contributions to old age security based on the insurance principle are unethical. I think that type of thing represents a form of swindle, and I want to demonstrate that by quoting a few figures. We know that the value of money has been declining all through modern history. To illustrate I wish to deal with a short table I have here. I have the complete table for one hundred years, and any member who wishes to see it is welcome to do so.
This is a table showing the purchasing value of the dollar as measured by the consumers' price index. It has been prepared by the Institute of Life Insurance, and for the year 1939 the dollar was taken as worth 100 cents. In terms of the dollar being worth 100 cents in 1939 the purchasing value in other years would be as follows:

This means that a person who commenced to pay into a fund for old age security in 1910, having paid in for forty years, would
Old Age Security
have put into the fund dollars worth 149-7 and would be paid today in dollars worth 59-1. I believe that is a sound argument against asking people to accept a contributory basis for old age security under the present money system. I do believe that current contributions are satisfactory, adequate and fair for current requirements such as health insurance, unemployment insurance, sick benefits and other current risks; but I repeat that anyone who has studied the history of money must realize that it is a form of swindle to ask people to contribute for old age security through the years on the insurance principle.
In further support of my argument I want to quote briefly from a news item from Washington appearing in the Christian Science Monitor of March 22:
Federal social security plan held unsound
A Brookings Institution official has hung tags "thoroughly unsound'' and "financially reckless" on the federal social security program. He urged a pay as you go system.
The spokesman was Lewis Meriam, vice-president of the foundation that carries on research into governmental activities. He told the Senate finance committee the old age and survivors' insurance program is "socially questionable".
From a public finance standpoint, Mr. Meriam testified, it is "thoroughly unsound."
The committee is studying a bill passed last year by the house to widen the coverage of the present social security act.
Calling the present program "financially reckless," he said:
"The old age and survivors' insurance system, as we have it today, saddles future generations of American citizens with a tremendous commitment for benefit payments in addition to other costs of government.
"The safe course is to adopt a true pay as you go system, giving such benefits as are reasonable and within our present economic ability, paying the costs each year, and trusting to future generations to do likewise."
He said the government has no "contractual obligation" to continue the present system.
"In our judgment it should make fundamental revision now before the present benefits are readjusted to offset the change in the cost of living." he added. "The present offers an opportunity to shift to a financially sound system that may not come again."
He said the law should provide benefits immediately for all persons in need because of old age or permanent disability . . .
The levy, he added, should be high enough to pay the expenses of the program year by year. And he said the money should be earmarked for this purpose.
Therefore I claim that for financial reasons alone it is unsound, unethical and unjust to establish old age security on the insurance principle through compulsory payments.
My second reason for supporting old age security from taxation is that under present conditions in Canada I believe any other method is impracticable, when we deal with

Old Age Security
old age security alone. It might not be so difficult if we had an over-all security plan, but knowing the large number of submarginal farmers operating in Canada, the low income groups in the cities, the widows and others with small incomes, I believe it would be impracticable and utterly unsound to attempt to collect on the basis of a contributory system. There would be the expense of accounting, the expense of administration, and the cost of investigation. As far as the old age pension means test is concerned, I understand the cost of investigation accounts for a large portion of the cost of administration in the field.
Before concluding I want to say a few words about our ability to meet the cost. I am shortening my remarks considerably because I know the minister wishes to conclude this debate this evening, so I am not going to deal at length with this matter though I had prepared some figures I thought were quite sound and logical. As to our ability to meet the cost, our gross national income from production is around $16,000 million. According to the minister's figures I understand the possible cost of paying old age pensions in Canada on the present basis but without a means test, at the age of seventy, would be about $300 million, or something less than $200 million more than our present costs. If paid at the age of sixty-five without a means test the cost would be about $391 million, which means additional $300 million would have to come from the federal exchequer. In the first place, the money paid to old age pensioners is returned to society. It goes into the hands of merchants, and then into labour and other costs incurred in production. That sounds like a large amount of money; but with our tremendous production I say it is simply a question of organizing that production to serve human beings first. I noticed that when the minister was dealing with the possible increase in the cost of old age pensions in the years to come he mentioned some substantial figures; but in quoting those figures he failed entirely to take note of the possibility of greatly increased production in the years immediately ahead. I believe that is a factor which must be considered when discussing the cost of old age pensions in the future.
I believe these costs can be met by the Canadian people, and would be met cheerfully if they were raised by the imposition of a tax as an addition to the income tax, based on ability to pay. I quite agree with other speakers that we do not get something for nothing; everything has to be paid for. But this cost, like other costs of government, would come out of production and our production
LMr. Herridge.l
can meet these costs. I understand that during the war we made gifts to other countries totalling over $3,000 million, and rightly so. Surely, Mr. Speaker, in times of peace, with our opportunities for greatly expanded production, we can do as much for our own people. If we could do this for others in wartime, we can give our senior citizens old age security today, paid out of taxation based on ability to pay. If this administration thought it was necessary to increase the defence estimates by two or three hundred million dollars, they would be increased without any question. The money would be provided, and this house would vote it. We can do the same in the war against poverty and insecure old age.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that this house, if it were concerned about providing old age security, could establish legislation, and could vote the money to see that our old age pensioners have security on a satisfactory basis without a means test. I hope the work of this committee will result in this government finally taking action to improve the position of the worthy section of our population which is entitled to old age security.

speechtext:
My anxiety, sir, is to see this committee struck, and to see it get down to work. I should like to see this committee do something about this problem; that is all that is concerning me. I am anxious about those with whom I have lived during the last forty years, who worked side by side with me, and who find themselves still working without too much security. I can think of 200; I can think of another 300; I can think of another 50 of them out in western Canada. Through no fault of their own, Mr. Speaker, perhaps because they have not been privileged to land on their feet, they find themselves getting older. Their wives, their brothers and sisters are all getting older; and they find themselves bereft of the security which you and I, sir, in this chamber have promised them for the last two or three years.
Now, let us get on with this job. Let us have this committee, and let us try to do something for those of our own age, and our own kind. Being the old man of Canada's House of Commons, it is easy enough for me to say that. I say it most sincerely. Eliminate the means test? Yes, for all of us who do not need to have a means test. Surely the committee can find some method of testing you and me, sir, and perhaps leave us outside the scheme. That is all right as far as I am concerned. I am thinking of those thousands and thousands of people who have been able to acquire for themselves only a modest home without a mortgage, and to raise a family. I

am thinking of them. Do not tie the means test to them. The income tax department has reports on the rest of us, and you can do as you like with us. Do not apply the means test to these men and women who have perhaps less than ten thousand to their credit. Let them go free. They paid the shot in Canada during their lifetime. Give them an opportunity.
I was interested, Mr. Speaker, in what the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) had to say. I agree with him one hundred per cent in what he said about those who went through northern Italy, Dieppe, and elsewhere. Such an experience added ten years to their lives, and I think they should receive special consideration. Let me go one step further than the member for Nanaimo. I am thinking, sir, of three different families whose boys did not come back. I saw the hair of the lady next door turn from a beautiful black to white within two weeks. A little farther up the street there is a family that lost two sons, and I saw that family age twenty years within two years. Ten doors down the street from where I live, I saw another lady's hair turn from black to grey, and from grey to white. I think the member for Nanaimo might add to the category which he enunciated so well a few minutes ago, those of our citizens who lost their boys overseas. Through no fault of their own, they find themselves aged from one to ten to twenty years almost overnight. I say to this committee that when it is established it should find some means of giving consideration to those people who find they are not as physically fit, not as strong as some of the rest of us. Let us have the committee set up. Let us get down to brass tacks.
I have another reason for requesting action on this matter. In my office tonight there are two different plans from organizations with which I am associated, and in my office at home there are three different plans, if not four, concerning some sort of pension scheme for employees for whom, as president of different companies, I happen to be responsible. Some of them are insurance company ideas. I have forgotten, for the moment, what the name of one is, but it is from some sort of economic adviser. We who are responsible for employees must of necessity give consideration to these plans. We must think about those who believe we are honest, and who look to us to provide them with their weekly pay envelopes; that is our responsibility. Yet, in the offing, there is this committee which this house has not got guts enough-

I believe Churchill said that was a proper word. If it is not a
Old Age Security
proper word I am sorry, sir, and I withdraw it. I am sorry if I have offended the finer sensibilities of some of those whose sensibilities are not as fine as some of the rest of us.

We do not want to clutter it up, Mr. Speaker, with large premiums which are being paid to men who sit in mahogany chairs behind mahogany desks, and take a rake-off from the premiums which employees and employers pay these insurance companies. I am not mentioning insurance companies particularly, but if the state is going into this business, then it should get into it and get going. It should give those of us who have the honour and privilege of signing payrolls a chance, not to get out from under our responsibility but to co-operate with you in the responsibilities which belong in this chamber, so that, in the final analysis, we can work out some sort of economy as a result of which our Canadian people will take new interest in their work, and will go to work and help this country of ours to the destiny which belongs to it.

speechtext:
Good. I could ask for nothing better. Keeping in mind the budget we had the other night, Liberals and Conservatives, I ask you to tell me how you are going to figure out the additional money necessary to remove the means test, increase the old age pension and reduce the pensionable age to 65 or 60. When you begin to tell me that, I will be an eager listener. Merely

to get up and say you want it done, with no suggestion as to how you are going to do it, remains just a weak futility. Let us face facts exactly as they are.
I am going to turn my attention for a few minutes to the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank). Unfortunately, he is not in his seat at the present time. I want to talk to that man. I think that probably I should include with him the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), because all those gentlemen are sure that the money must come out of the taxpayer. If that is the case, they are right in accord with the Minister of Finance. They have no criticism of his budget or of his means of building a budget. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre this afternoon said that he had given considerable attention to the proposals of Social Credit and that he was quite convinced that there was in Social Credit not nearly as much sense as there was moonshine. It might be suggested that, generally speaking, a man finds what he goes out to hunt; hence I presume the hon. member has been spending a good deal of time in hunting moonshine. I am going to propound a suggestion for the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Social Crediters are not going to take this nonsense lying down. In the Social Credit group are men who are just about as well informed on economics and finance as any that are to be found in Canada, and they are not going to take the silly remarks of a lot of half-baked people without having something to say about it.
In the first place something must be done to discover how to make what is physically possible financially possible, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) pointed out this afternoon. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had nothing to say about that. I suppose he agrees, and I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West would agree-that is what I gathered from what he had to 'say-that all we need to do is to increase production and we can take the money out of the production. I will ask him how much he would have to increase the fruit production of British Columbia in order to get any more money out of it, when he cannot sell what he now can produce. That is the question. Just as soon as we get to the point at which we are producing all we can sell, to increase production brings down the price under the present financial system and decreases the money you can get out of the goods. Let us face that fact

and put aside the nonsense. Let us remember that this parliament was elected to govern this country, not to talk nonsense. If the country is demanding that the old age pensionable age shall be reduced to 65, that the means tests shall be abolished and that the pension shall be increased, it is our business to find out how to do that. If we cannot do it under the system we are using today, we had then better begin to examine some other system.
Let us consider any one of the commodities you wish to name. We in Canada of course have not a great many surpluses. But down in the United States-and all hon. members are familiar with what is going on down there-there is in the neighbourhood of $4 billion worth of surplus agricultural products ranging over something like twenty different commodities. Can anybody tell anyone in the United States how they can increase the amount of money they can get by increasing the production of any one of these commodities or of twenty of them? As a matter of fact, every increase they make in such things as soya beans, cotton, wheat, oats, barley, rye, peanuts, and a whole lot of other things, weakens the state, because there is danger of a collapse in prices, and tends to decrease the amount of money they can collect from the people producing them. That is the kind of thing the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) must face.
What do you find when you face it? We find in the United States this remarkable thing. We find $4 billion worth of surplus goods already in the possession of the government, bought as surplus to keep the price structure from going down; and it is being held at a colossal cost to the nation. They have already appropriated, or they are thinking of appropriating, $2 billion more to buy the surpluses of next year. Will anybody, including the hon. member for Vancouver East, tell us how they are going to get money out of that production? They put money into that production, not get it out. In other words, an increase in production does not increase the amount of money available to the state beyond a certain amount unless they can sell the produce. These are cold facts.
Now, according to the information I have, at the very time when the United States has a surplus production of so many different kinds, they are talking of decreasing their military appropriation by $2 billion because they cannot afford the $2 billion. If you can think of anything more fantastically absurd than an attitude like that you will be doing
Oid Age Security
wonderfully well. You will have to think about it in a nightmare, because no intelligent person can concede that a nation that can produce more of every kind of thing than they can possibly use, with a surplus of everything, cannot afford to have defence.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE TO STUDY LEGISLATION, ALTERNATIVE METHODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, it is simple. It is just as simple as it is to breathe, but there are a lot of simpletons who have not got sense enough even to breathe right.
In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, there are three things which need to be done this year without further delay. In this respect I agree with the other hon. members who have

spoken. There simply must be an increase in the pension. The age must be lowered to at least 65 and the means test must be progressively eliminated. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Acadia and several other hon. members today, to give substantial old age pensions all over the country would have a powerful influence on the production in Canada, because it would provide a market and certainly would have a tremendous influence on our consumption and a very material influence on employment in the country, because the pensioners would be able to buy the goods which we are able to produce. It would provide for us a market. ,
There is a greater urgency for this increase of old age pensions and the spreading out of the pension over a wider area of population than some people realize. The age of the machines, which is rapidly developing against our generation, is putting more and more people out of work. For a good deal of time there has been opposition to that idea. Men have been trying to establish that machines do not put people out of work; that they actually increase the work which is available. Even the most hard-headed and reactionary thinkers in the United States are beginning to discover that the machines actually are putting men out of work. I hold in my hand a clipping from a newspaper or a periodical called Labour, which I think all hon. members receive. This issue is dated March 18,
1950.	Here is an article on finance based upon findings of two of the best authorities in the United States. First of all we find the heading, "Higher efficiency blamed for addition of 750,000 to ranks of jobless". That is in the United States. The article states:
This startling testimony came from J. A. Livingston, financial columnist, who is syndicated in many conservative papers, and from the magazine Business Week. Neither can be remotely regarded as "radical".
"Production efficiency cuts jobs" was the headline on a column by Livingston. Then he went on to say: "Efficiency is beginning to creep upon us . . . you can see it in the unemployment statistics." He

highest in nine years.
In part, Livingston said, this is because "Post-war technological improvements are coming home to roost." Industries of all kinds, including the railroads, have installed labour-saving devices, and now "these improvements begin to pay off"-in layoff of workers.
"Fewer men or less time are now required to do the same job," he declared.
In the past year, unemployment rose by 1,500,000 and Livingston estimated that "half of that is attributable to higher output per worker." In short, labour's higher productivity has caused a loss of 750,000 jobs in one year.
Very bluntly Livingston put this question: "Will increased efficiency raise hell with full employment?"

Well, that is pretty serious, in the light of the situation which confronts us. The condition is very much like that in Canada. Further down I cull this from the article: "Magazine Echoes Warning"
Business Week, a leading organ of industry, made the same point-in perhaps even stronger terms. It did so in a lead article entitled "Unemployment, prosperity: Strange Pair."
"Labour productivity is rising-rising fast." the magazine said. " A Business Week survey confirmed that fact beyond question. It's taking fewer workers each year to produce our high volume of goods-so unemployment is creeping up."
Hence, "there's an unemployment problem again
__even though the business boom is going full
blast."
Output of goods and services in 1949 was about $259 billion, about the same as for 1948, after adjustment for price differences, the magazine explained.
"But in 1949 it took 3 per cent fewer workers to produce that output," it said.
In agriculture also, "the trend toward higher and higher production per worker is striking." Since 1947, employment on the farms has been dropping while production "has been as high as ever," the magazine reported.
The truth which is borne out in this article I have read is a very solemn truth. It indicates we have simply got to find some way or other of making the goods we are able to produce pay off in terms of finance, so that we can help those who are being displaced by machinery. This is having a very important effect on the old people, and it makes it more and more necessary that we be able to give munificently to those who are displaced after reaching the age of sixty-five years, and those who have reached the age of seventy.
An interesting article along the same lines appears in the Ottawa Evening Citizen, home edition, page 6, for March 16. In that article a United States scientist visualizes machines running the world in twenty years or less. Professor Norbert Wiener, the famous American mathematician, spoke in this fashion before an audience in the national research council auditorium at Ottawa on March 15. His speech is reported in the article of which I have given the head note. He says the time will come when we will displace men on a far greater scale than they are now being displaced. He says that the machine could take over a whole chemical plant, and that the du Ponts are doing it now, with an oilcracking plant. He states further that the automatic factory can be used in manufacturing automobiles.
The meaning of all this is the same as the meaning of the evidence set out by Mr. Livingston and Business Week. It means that we shall be able to have plenty of production, but with fewer and fewer men, which means that man will be disposed of at an earlier age, so that probably by the time he
Old Age Security
reaches the age of fifty or fifty-five it will be no longer possible for him to obtain a job. And if we are unable to give a man a job, unquestionably we have to find some means of giving him a living without a job. That is just as simple and as clear as a star in a starlit, clear sky.
What are we going to do about it? Are we going to wait until the problem develops to such an extent that we can do nothing about it, or are we going to go into the matter now, closely, while yet there is time?
The percentage of our population made up of people sixty-five years of age and over is rapidly increasing, as was indicated this afternoon by one hon. member. In an article appearing in the Ottawa Journal of recent date we find the heading "Sixty-five too young to retire", a statement attributed to Glen R. Shepherd, M.D.
In this article are some figures which I am sure hon. members would find interesting if, in their busy lives, they may have overlooked them. These figures show that in 1940 there were 9,200,000 people in the United States more than sixty-five years old, and it is said that in 1980 there will be at least 18,501,000 who will reach that age. But the working ages of twenty to fifty-nine will not increase one bit. How are the increasing numbers of people over sixty-five years of age to live off the static or decreasing number of producers?
This is another problem which faces us. We are right up against it; we cannot sidestep it. What are we going to do about it? It is all involved in this matter of making financially possible that which is physically possible, and finding money from some source other than taxation. There is no question that we can produce the goods-all the goods we need. There has never been any doubt about our ability to do that. But to get money out of those goods is going to be our problem and that is the thing we are discussing tonight. There should not be a bit of difficulty in having those people in the United States who are able to produce support the 18 million people in 1980 over the age of sixty-five years, to whom I have referred, if the goods they could produce could be turned into money to support those people. They will be able to produce the goods.
We must find the means whereby we can translate goods into terms of money, and there is no conceivable way except through the use of debt-free money, as Social Crediters have advised and advocated, and as the Guernsey islanders demonstrated in their famous experiment of 1815.
There is no question whatever that we can pay adequate pensions in Canada. I do not

Old Age Security
doubt for one moment that our Canadian economy can produce more goods by far than our old age pensioners could possibly use, including all the people over sixty-five and all the people over fifty-five, if we have to put them all out of work, if we had just time enough to expand our economy, as we can do, and if we once get to the point where we can be realistic and turn into money the goods we are able to produce.
I have a letter here from which I should like to quote some excerpts. I think nearly every member received it. This letter is dated March 20, 1950, and comes from the office of the ex-chairman of the Welland county board of old age pensions and mothers' allowances, at Fort Erie, Ontario. This letter indicates that the writer of it has no doubt whatever that we can organize affairs in this country so that we can pay all old age pensioners, without a means test, a good pension. In the second paragraph he says:
The total expense involved in this welfare service must amount to more than one-half of the cost of the actual pensions themselves-with all the machinery necessary in paying of same-and the initial and periodic investigations which many times cause real heartache to some of these elderly people who are afraid to earn an extra dollar in case they have it deducted from their cheque.
Taking everything into consideration-the number now employed in keeping records, the expense of office equipment, furniture and supplies essential under the present system, I feel that it would be far cheaper to the country and more satisfactory to the pensioner if the following plan were in effect.
When any person becomes seventy years old, he should send proof of age to the board at Ottawa with his application for pension. (Ottawa has the census records for checking.) The board could then issue in his favour a book of twelve cheques, dated one for each month-with an application blank for renewal inserted before the November cheque to be mailed to Ottawa then. This book should be taken immediately to any chartered bank and left there so that on the first day of each month, the pensioner could go to the bank, endorse his cheque for that month and receive his money.
Under this system, all provincial and local boards, investigators, etc., would be eliminated. The old age pension should be paid to all persons, regardless of their financial condition, when they become seventy years of age (it should be sixty-five). I "firmly believe that this proposed system would actually save the country money, and at the same time wipe out a great deal of the present dissatisfaction on the part of pensioners and provide comfort for many who really need it but are doing without under the present system.
There is a man who gives us hope even under the present system, under our way of doing business now. I think I am perfectly within the bounds of moderation when I contend that the old age pension must be increased, the pensionable age must be brought down to sixty-five, and the means test must be progressively removed. There is no need to have a committee to do that. If a committee is appointed to find ways and means of doing the thing we all know we
[Mr. Blackmore.l
ought to do, that is a different matter. Then the resolution should be so worded as to say that; but it is not so worded. In fact, I suspect that when the committee is in session if anyone were to attend and try to explain to the committee how Social Credit would be able to solve the problem he would not be given a respectful hearing at all. It would be a wonder if he were not ruled out of order by the chairman. Nevertheless, whether or not members of the house are prepared to back proposals to use debt-free money to finance what is physically possible, the simple fact remains that beyond any question it is the duty and responsibility of this house to see that these three objectives are achieved, namely: increase in the old age pension to make it adequate for the needs of the times; the reduction of the age to sixty-five; and the progressive elemination of the means test.
